`taskrun` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/taskrun.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.

Two directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.

`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.

`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.

`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.

A task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. The first watched path with a reason decides that the task runs, and the reason is `new <path>` when the snapshot records no digest for it, `missing <path>` when the snapshot records one but the workspace has no such file, and `changed <path>` when the file's digest differs from the recorded one; a file whose digest matches gives no reason. A task no watched path condemns runs anyway when some dependency runs, with the reason `needs <dep>` naming the lexicographically smallest dependency that runs, so a path reason always wins over a dependency one. `plan` prints one line per task in the order `order` prints, `run <name> <reason>` or `skip <name>`, and then a final line `total run=<r> skip=<s>` counting the two. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

content.text:
# taskrun

A dependency-aware task runner with no dependencies of its own. It reads a task file from standard input and answers questions about it; it never executes a command.

## Layout

| File | What it owns |
| --- | --- |
| `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
| `src/parse.js` | the task-file grammar and the refusals it words, as `ParseError` |
| `src/graph.js` | run order over the dependency edges |
| `src/digest.js` | the FNV-1a digest the snapshot format records |

`test/taskrun.test.js` is the suite for what is already here. `data/files/` holds the workspace files the examples name, and `data/snapshots/` the digest snapshots.

## The task file

One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace.

```
# build.tasks
task build node build.js
task bundle node bundle.js
needs bundle build
```

`task <name> <word>...` declares a task whose command is the remaining words joined with single spaces. `needs <name> <dependency>...` adds dependencies; a repeated edge counts once, and a `needs` line may stand before the `task` line it names.

## Modes

- `order` prints the task names one per line, in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose dependencies have all been printed.
- `show <name>` prints `<name>: <command>` and then `needs: ` followed by the dependencies in ascending order, or `-` when there are none.
- `digest <path>...` prints `<path> <digest>` for each path in argument order, with `missing` in place of a digest for a path that is not there. The digest is 32-bit FNV-1a over the file's bytes — offset basis `0x811c9dc5`, prime `16777619`, xor then multiply — as eight lowercase hex digits.

## Failures

Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A parse failure names its 1-based input line: `error: line 2: unknown directive run`. The messages are `expected task <name> <word>...`, `expected needs <name> <dependency>...`, `invalid task name <name>`, `task <name> is declared twice` and `unknown directive <word>`. A `needs` line naming a task no `task` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown task <name>`, and so is `show` on such a name.

## Known gaps

`order` does not detect a dependency cycle: it stops as soon as nothing is ready and leaves every task in the cycle out of its output. The task file has no way to declare which files a task reads or writes, so nothing here can tell whether a task is up to date.

1: /** The task-file parser: directives to tasks, with the failures the specification words. */
2: 
3: const NAME = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: 
5: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line it was read from, or 0 when it names none. */
6: export class ParseError extends Error {
7:   /**
8:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names no line.
9:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the `error: ` prefix.
10:    */
11:   constructor(line, message) {
12:     super(message)
13:     this.name = 'ParseError'
14:     this.line = line
15:   }
16: }
17: 
18: /** Whether a word is a usable task name. */
19: function isName(word) {
20:   return NAME.test(word)
21: }
22: 
23: /**
24:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
25:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
26:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
27:  */
28: export function splitLines(text) {
29:   const split = text.split('\n')
30:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
31:   return split
32: }
33: 
34: /**
35:  * Parse a task file into its tasks.
36:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
37:  * @returns {Map<string, {name: string, command: string, needs: string[]}>} the tasks by name, in declaration order.
38:  */
39: export function parse(lines) {
40:   const tasks = new Map()
41:   const referenced = []
42:   const attachments = []
43:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
44:     const line = index + 1
45:     const text = raw.trim()
46:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
47:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
48:     if (words[0] === 'task') {
49:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, 'expected task <name> <word>...')
50:       const name = words[1]
51:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
52:       if (tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `task ${name} is declared twice`)
53:       tasks.set(name, { name, command: words.slice(2).join(' '), needs: [] })
54:     } else if (words[0] === 'needs') {
55:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, 'expected needs <name> <dependency>...')
56:       const [, name, ...values] = words
57:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
58:       referenced.push(name)
59:       for (const value of values) {
60:         if (!isName(value)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${value}`)
61:         referenced.push(value)
62:       }
63:       attachments.push({ name, values })
64:     } else {
65:       throw new ParseError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
66:     }
67:   }
68:   for (const name of referenced) {
69:     if (!tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(0, `unknown task ${name}`)
70:   }
71:   for (const { name, values } of attachments) {
72:     const list = tasks.get(name).needs
73:     for (const value of values) {
74:       if (!list.includes(value)) list.push(value)
75:     }
76:   }
77:   return tasks
78: }

1: /** Ordering the task graph. */
2: 
3: /**
4:  * The tasks in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose
5:  * dependencies have all been emitted. A cycle has no such task, so the order
6:  * stops early and leaves the tasks in it out.
7:  * @param {Map<string, {needs: string[]}>} tasks - the parsed tasks.
8:  * @returns {string[]} the names in run order.
9:  */
10: export function order(tasks) {
11:   const remaining = new Set(tasks.keys())
12:   const emitted = new Set()
13:   const out = []
14:   while (remaining.size > 0) {
15:     const ready = [...remaining].filter(name => tasks.get(name).needs.every(need => emitted.has(need))).sort()
16:     if (ready.length === 0) break
17:     remaining.delete(ready[0])
18:     emitted.add(ready[0])
19:     out.push(ready[0])
20:   }
21:   return out
22: }

Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.\n\nTwo directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.\n\n`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.\n\n`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.\n\n`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. `taskrun` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/taskrun.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.

Two directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.

`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.

`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.

`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.

A task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. The first watched path with a reason decides that the task runs, and the reason is `new <path>` when the snapshot records no digest for it, `missing <path>` when the snapshot records one but the workspace has no such file, and `changed <path>` when the file's digest differs from the recorded one; a file whose digest matches gives no reason. A task no watched path condemns runs anyway when some dependency runs, with the reason `needs <dep>` naming the lexicographically smallest dependency that runs, so a path reason always wins over a dependency one. `plan` prints one line per task in the order `order` prints, `run <name> <reason>` or `skip <name>`, and then a final line `total run=<r> skip=<s>` counting the two. `src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `merge`, `merge2` or `regions`, and reads three documents from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; a line that is exactly `%%%` separates the documents, and every other line belongs to the document it sits in. The three documents, in order, are mine, the base they both derive from, and theirs. A document may hold no line at all. Exit 0 when the merge is clean and 1 when any conflict was written, on every mode.

Compare each side against the base with a longest common subsequence over whole lines, comparing them as exact strings. When two subsequences are equally long, take the one whose matches come earliest: walking both documents from the start, take a match whenever the two current lines are equal, and otherwise advance the side whose remaining subsequence is at least as long as the other's, preferring to advance the base when they tie. Every stretch the subsequence does not cover is a change, described as a run of base lines replaced by a run of that side's lines; an insertion replaces zero base lines and a deletion inserts zero lines.

Gather the changes from both sides into one list ordered by where they start in the base, with the changes from mine before the changes from theirs when they start at the same place. Walk that list: take the first remaining change, let the region run from its base start to its base end, and keep absorbing the next change while that change starts at or before the region's current end, extending the end to cover it. The base lines before a region and after the last one form stable regions, which the merge keeps unchanged.

A region only one change touches resolves to that side's lines. For a region several changes touch, each side's replacement runs from the smallest start of its own changes, moved back by however far the region begins before those changes do in the base, to the largest end of its own changes, moved forward by however far the region ends after them. With mine's lines, the base lines of the region, and theirs's lines in hand: if mine and theirs are equal the region resolves to mine; otherwise if mine equals the base it resolves to theirs; otherwise if theirs equals the base it resolves to mine; otherwise the region is a conflict.

`merge` prints the resolved lines in order, and writes a conflict as the line `<<<<<<< mine`, then mine's lines, then `||||||| base`, then the base's lines, then `=======`, then theirs's lines, then `>>>>>>> theirs`. `merge2` writes the same thing without the `||||||| base` line and the base's lines. `regions` instead prints one line per region: `stable N`, `mine N`, `theirs N` or `both N`, where N counts the lines the region resolves to and `both` names a region where the two sides made the same change, or `conflict mine=A base=O theirs=B` with the three line counts.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output. goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `merge`, `merge2` or `regions`, and reads three documents from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; a line that is exactly `%%%` separates the documents, and every other line belongs to the document it sits in. The three documents, in order, are mine, the base they both derive from, and theirs. A document may hold no line at all. Exit 0 when the merge is clean and 1 when any conflict was written, on every mode.

Compare each side against the base with a longest common subsequence over whole lines, comparing them as exact strings. When two subsequences are equally long, take the one whose matches come earliest: walking both documents from the start, take a match whenever the two current lines are equal, and otherwise advance the side whose remaining subsequence is at least as long as the other's, preferring to advance the base when they tie. Every stretch the subsequence does not cover is a change, described as a run of base lines replaced by a run of that side's lines; an insertion replaces zero base lines and a deletion inserts zero lines.

Gather the changes from both sides into one list ordered by where they start in the base, with the changes from mine before the changes from theirs when they start at the same place. Walk that list: take the first remaining change, let the region run from its base start to its base end, and keep absorbing the next change while that change starts at or before the region's current end, extending the end to cover it. The base lines before a region and after the last one form stable regions, which the merge keeps unchanged.

A region only one change touches resolves to that side's lines. For a region several changes touch, each side's replacement runs from the smallest start of its own changes, moved back by however far the region begins before those changes do in the base, to the largest end of its own changes, moved forward by however far the region ends after them. With mine's lines, the base lines of the region, and theirs's lines in hand: if mine and theirs are equal the region resolves to mine; otherwise if mine equals the base it resolves to theirs; otherwise if theirs equals the base it resolves to mine; otherwise the region is a conflict.

`merge` prints the resolved lines in order, and writes a conflict as the line `<<<<<<< mine`, then mine's lines, then `||||||| base`, then the base's lines, then `=======`, then theirs's lines, then `>>>>>>> theirs`. `merge2` writes the same thing without the `||||||| base` line and the base's lines. `regions` instead prints one line per region: `stable N`, `mine N`, `theirs N` or `both N`, where N counts the lines the region resolves to and `both` names a region where the two sides made the same change, or `conflict mine=A base=O theirs=B` with the three line counts.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js merge|merge2|regions` when the argument is not exactly one of the three mode words, and `error: expected three parts separated by %%%` when the input does not hold exactly three documents. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `tokens` or `stats`, reads UTF-8 source text from standard input, and scans it. Exit 0 when the whole input scans.

Positions count from 1. Reading a line feed moves to the next line and sets the column back to 1. Reading a tab moves the column forward to the next multiple of 4 plus 1, so a tab in column 1 lands on column 5 and a tab in column 6 lands on column 9. Every other code point moves the column forward by 1. A token's position is where its first code point sits.

Spaces, tabs, carriage returns and line feeds separate tokens and produce none. `//` starts a comment that runs to the next line feed or to the end of the input. `/*` starts a block comment that ends at the matching `*/` and nests, so `/* a /* b */ c */` is one comment; a block comment that never closes is an error reported at the `/*` that opened the outermost one.

An identifier starts with a letter or `_` and continues with letters, digits and `_`; it is a `keyword` when it is exactly `let`, `if`, `else`, `while`, `return`, `true`, `false` or `null`, and an `ident` otherwise. A `number` starts with a digit. `0x` or `0X` introduces hexadecimal digits, `0b` or `0B` binary, and `0o` or `0O` octal; anything else is decimal digits, optionally a `.` and more digits, and optionally `e` or `E`, an optional `+` or `-`, and more digits. A `.` only continues a number when a digit follows it, and an exponent marker only continues one when a digit, or a sign and then a digit, follows it. A `_` may sit between two digits of the same run and nowhere else. A number followed immediately by a letter, a digit or `_` that the rules above did not consume, and a prefix with no digit after it, are both errors, and the reported text is everything the scanner ran through, up to and including those trailing characters.

A `string` is written between double quotes and carries the escapes `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\\`, `\"`, `\0`, `\xHH` with exactly two hexadecimal digits, and `\u{H...}` with at least one hexadecimal digit naming a code point of at most 10FFFF. Any other escape is an error reported at its backslash. A line feed inside a string is an error reported where the line feed sits, and a string the input ends before closing is an error reported at its opening quote. A `rawstring` is written `r"` then any characters, line feeds included, up to the first `"`; it carries no escapes, its position is that of the `r`, and an input that ends before the closing `"` is an `unterminated string` reported at that `r` rather than at the quote after it.

The punctuation, matched longest first, is `==`, `!=`, `<=`, `>=`, `&&`, `||`, `->`, `=>`, `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `=`, `<`, `>`, `!`, `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[`, `]`, `,`, `;` and `.`. Any other character is an error.

`tokens` prints one line per token, `<line>:<column> <kind> <body>`. For a `string` and a `rawstring` the body is the decoded value written as a JSON string, quotes and escapes included; for every other kind it is the source text of the token. `stats` instead prints one line per kind, `<kind> <count>`, for all six kinds `ident`, `keyword`, `number`, `punct`, `rawstring` and `string` in that order, whether or not any token had that kind, and then `total N`.

15:   if (mode !== 'tokens' && mode !== 'stats') {
16:     process.stderr.write('error: usage: cli.js tokens|stats\n')
17:     process.exit(2)
18:   }
19: 
20:   let source
21:   try {
22:     source = fs.readFileSync(0, 'utf8')
23:   } catch (e) {
24:     source = ''
25:   }

28:   try {
29:     tokens = scan(source)
30:   } catch (e) {
31:     if (e instanceof LexError) {
32:       process.stderr.write(`error: ${e.line}:${e.col}: ${e.reason}\n`)
33:       process.exit(2)
34:     }
35:     throw e
36:   }
37:

41:       out += `${t.line}:${t.col} ${t.kind} ${t.text}\n`
42:     }

46:     for (const t of tokens) counts[t.kind]++
47:     let out = ''
48:     for (const k of STAT_KINDS) out += `${k} ${counts[k]}\n`
49:     out += `total ${tokens.length}\n`
50:     process.stdout.write(out)

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `tokens` or `stats`, reads UTF-8 source text from standard input, and scans it. Exit 0 when the whole input scans.

Positions count from 1. Reading a line feed moves to the next line and sets the column back to 1. Reading a tab moves the column forward to the next multiple of 4 plus 1, so a tab in column 1 lands on column 5 and a tab in column 6 lands on column 9. Every other code point moves the column forward by 1. A token's position is where its first code point sits.

Spaces, tabs, carriage returns and line feeds separate tokens and produce none. `//` starts a comment that runs to the next line feed or to the end of the input. `/*` starts a block comment that ends at the matching `*/` and nests, so `/* a /* b */ c */` is one comment; a block comment that never closes is an error reported at the `/*` that opened the outermost one.

An identifier starts with a letter or `_` and continues with letters, digits and `_`; it is a `keyword` when it is exactly `let`, `if`, `else`, `while`, `return`, `true`, `false` or `null`, and an `ident` otherwise. A `number` starts with a digit. `0x` or `0X` introduces hexadecimal digits, `0b` or `0B` binary, and `0o` or `0O` octal; anything else is decimal digits, optionally a `.` and more digits, and optionally `e` or `E`, an optional `+` or `-`, and more digits. A `.` only continues a number when a digit follows it, and an exponent marker only continues one when a digit, or a sign and then a digit, follows it. A `_` may sit between two digits of the same run and nowhere else. A number followed immediately by a letter, a digit or `_` that the rules above did not consume, and a prefix with no digit after it, are both errors, and the reported text is everything the scanner ran through, up to and including those trailing characters.

A `string` is written between double quotes and carries the escapes `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\\`, `\"`, `\0`, `\xHH` with exactly two hexadecimal digits, and `\u{H...}` with at least one hexadecimal digit naming a code point of at most 10FFFF. Any other escape is an error reported at its backslash. A line feed inside a string is an error reported where the line feed sits, and a string the input ends before closing is an error reported at its opening quote. A `rawstring` is written `r"` then any characters, line feeds included, up to the first `"`; it carries no escapes, its position is that of the `r`, and an input that ends before the closing `"` is an `unterminated string` reported at that `r` rather than at the quote after it.

The punctuation, matched longest first, is `==`, `!=`, `<=`, `>=`, `&&`, `||`, `->`, `=>`, `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `=`, `<`, `>`, `!`, `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[`, `]`, `,`, `;` and `.`. Any other character is an error.

`tokens` prints one line per token, `<line>:<column> <kind> <body>`. For a `string` and a `rawstring` the body is the decoded value written as a JSON string, quotes and escapes included; for every other kind it is the source text of the token. `stats` instead prints one line per kind, `<kind> <count>`, for all six kinds `ident`, `keyword`, `number`, `punct`, `rawstring` and `string` in that order, whether or not any token had that kind, and then `total N`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The message is `error: usage: cli.js tokens|stats` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: <line>:<column>: <reason>` where the reason is one of `unterminated string`, `newline in string`, `unterminated block comment`, `invalid escape \<character>`, `invalid number <text>` and `unexpected character <character>`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

It reads a document from standard input and writes HTML, or the document's outline, to standard output. 4: 5: ## Layout 6: 7: | File | What it owns | 8: | --- | --- | 9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported | 10: | `src/block.js` | the block grammar — fences, headings, lists, paragraphs — and the rendering of each | 11: | `src/inline.js` | the inline grammar: escapes, code spans, emphasis, and links | 12: | `src/html.js` | `escapeText` and `escapeAttribute` | 13: 14: `test/mdlite.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the link-definition files the examples name. 15: 16: ## Blocks 17: 18: The document is split on newlines and the empty tail a trailing newline leaves is dropped. A line is then read as one of these, in this order. 19: 20: A line of three or more backticks with no further backtick on it opens a fenced code block, and its info string is the rest of the line, trimmed, of which the first word is used. The fence closes at the first later line that is nothing but backticks, at least as many as the opening had, and everything between the two is content. A fence that never closes fails. A blank line ends whatever block was open. `#` to `######` followed by a space is a heading of that level, over the trimmed rest of the line. `- ` at the very start of a line is a bullet item, unless a paragraph is already open, in which case it is one of that paragraph's lines. Anything else is a paragraph line, trimmed. 21: 22: Each block renders to `

` to `

`, `

` with its lines joined by newlines, `

    ` with one `
  • ` per item on its own line, or `
    ` with the content copied in, `class="language-"` when there is an info string. The blocks are joined with newlines and the output ends with one; an empty document renders nothing at all.
23: 
24: ## Inline
25: 
26: A backslash before one of `` \ ` * [ ] ( ) `` writes that character literally. A backtick pair is a code span, with its content escaped. `**` pairs make `` and `*` pairs make ``, each rendering its content inline. `[text](url)` is a link, with the text rendered inline and the url escaped for the attribute. An unmatched marker is literal text. Everything else is escaped for HTML.
27: 
28: ## Modes
29: 
30: - `html` writes the rendered document.
31: - `outline` writes one line per heading, ` `.
32: 
33: ## Failures
34: 
35: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. An unterminated fence is `error: line N: unterminated code fence`, naming the line the fence opened on. A malformed argument list is refused with the usage line.
36: 
37: ## Known gaps
38: 
39: A list is flat: an indented `- ` is a paragraph line, not a nested item. There are no reference links, so `[text][label]` is literal text and a `[label]: url` line renders as a paragraph. Fence content is copied out verbatim, so a `<` in a code block escapes into the surrounding HTML and a document that shows HTML in a code block renders wrong.

1: #!/usr/bin/env node
2: /** The command: `html` and `outline`, each over the document on standard input. */
3: 
4: import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
5: import { BlockError, headings, parse, render, splitLines } from './block.js'
6: 
7: const USAGE = 'usage: cli.js html|outline'
8: 
9: /** Report one failure the way the specification words it, and stop. */
10: function fail(message) {
11:   process.stderr.write(`error: ${message}\n`)
12:   process.exit(2)
13: }
14: 
15: const argv = process.argv.slice(2)
16: const mode = argv[0]
17: if (!['html', 'outline'].includes(mode) || argv.length !== 1) fail(USAGE)
18: 
19: let parsed
20: try {
21:   parsed = parse(splitLines(readFileSync(0, 'utf8')))
22: } catch (error) {
23:   if (!(error instanceof BlockError)) throw error
24:   fail(`line ${error.line}: ${error.message}`)
25: }
26: 
27: if (mode === 'html') {
28:   process.stdout.write(render(parsed))
29: } else {
30:   process.stdout.write(headings(parsed).map(one => `${one.level} ${one.text}\n`).join(''))
31: }

content.text:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `values` or `deps`, and reads a sheet from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. From each line strip the leading spaces and tabs; ignore the line when nothing is left or when what is left begins with `#`. Otherwise the address runs to the next space or tab or to the end of the line, one run of spaces and tabs is skipped, and the rest of the line, verbatim, is the cell's content. Exit 0 whenever the sheet parses.

An address is one or two letters naming a column and one to three digits naming a row, upper-cased when read, so `a1` and `A1` are one cell; columns run `A` to `Z` and then `AA` to `ZZ`, and the row is at least 1. Cells print in ascending column order and, within a column, ascending row order.

Content that begins with `=` is a formula; anything else is a literal. A literal that is empty, or a cell nobody declared, is the number 0. A literal that matches an optional `-`, digits, and optionally a `.` and more digits is that number. A literal that is exactly one of the error tokens `#DIV/0!`, `#REF!`, `#VALUE!`, `#CYCLE!`, `#NAME?` and `#ERR!` is that error. Everything else is text.

A formula body holds numbers written as digits with an optional `.` and more digits and no sign and no exponent, cell addresses, ranges written `A1:B3`, the bare words `TRUE` and `FALSE`, function calls, parentheses, and the operators `^`, `*`, `/`, `+`, `-`, `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Spaces and tabs may sit anywhere between tokens. Names are read case-insensitively. Precedence, loosest first, is the comparisons, then `+` and `-`, then `*` and `/`, then `^`, and then a leading `-` or `+`; the comparisons and the additive and multiplicative operators group to the left, `^` groups to the right, and a leading sign binds tighter than `^`, so `-2^2` is 4 and `2^3^2` is 512. Anything the grammar does not accept makes the cell `#ERR!`, and so does a range written anywhere but directly as a function argument, which the grammar does accept. A word the grammar accepts that is neither `TRUE`, `FALSE` nor the name of a call is read as a cell address, and one that is not one or two letters and one to three digits naming a row of at least 1 — `AAA1`, `A1000`, `A0` and `FOO` alike — is an address outside the addressable range rather than a grammar failure.

The functions are `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT` and `AVG`, each taking one or more arguments, `ABS` taking exactly one, and `IF` taking exactly three. A call with the wrong number of arguments is `#ERR!` and a call to any other name is `#NAME?`. An argument that is a range contributes every cell it covers, in ascending column and then ascending row order, whichever corner it was written from. `SUM` totals, `MIN` and `MAX` pick, `AVG` totals and divides by how many values it saw, and `COUNT` reports how many of its values are numbers. Every one of them but `COUNT` reads each value it takes as a number, so `ABS`, `SUM`, `MIN`, `MAX` and `AVG` take text as `#VALUE!` rather than ordering or ignoring it. `IF` reads its first argument as a condition, taking `TRUE` and a non-zero number as true and `FALSE` and zero as false, and returns only the branch it takes, so an error in the other branch is invisible.

A value is a number, text, a boolean, or an error. In an arithmetic position a boolean is 1 or 0 and text is `#VALUE!`. Division by a zero divisor is `#DIV/0!`, and so is any arithmetic result that is not finite. A comparison compares two numbers numerically, two texts by code point, and two booleans with false below true; across kinds every number is below every text and every text is below every boolean. An address outside the addressable range is `#REF!`. A cell whose evaluation reaches itself, directly or through other cells, is `#CYCLE!`. An error reaching an operator or a function is the result: for an operator the left operand's error wins over the right one's, and for a function the first error among the arguments read left to right, ranges expanded, wins over everything else, including over `COUNT` counting.

`values` prints `<address>=<value>` for every declared cell. A number prints as JavaScript would print it after being rounded to ten significant digits, an error prints as its token, a boolean prints as `TRUE` or `FALSE`, and text prints as itself. `deps` instead prints `<address>:` followed by ` <address>` for every distinct cell the content names directly, ranges expanded, ordered by column and then by row; only addresses inside the addressable range are named. A literal names none, and so does a formula the grammar does not accept; a formula the grammar accepts names its cells whatever the cell evaluates to, so a misplaced range still names every cell it covers.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js values|deps` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, `error: line N: invalid cell address <address>`, and `error: line N: cell <address> is declared twice`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

## Summary

I implemented the spreadsheet evaluator across several modules under `src/`:

- **`src/address.js`** — column/row conversions and strict address-shape validation (1–2 letters, 1–3 digit row ≥ 1).
- **`src/tokenizer.js`** — lexes formula bodies into numbers, identifiers (letters + optional digits, used for addresses/keywords/function names), operators (longest-match first for `<=`, `>=`, `<>`), parens, comma, colon.
- **`src/parser.js`** — recursive-descent parser implementing the precedence chain (comparisons → `+`/`-` → `*`/`/` → `^` right-assoc → unary sign tightest), with a special `parseArgument` that only recognizes `WORD:WORD` ranges directly as function arguments (anywhere else a colon leads to a grammar failure → `#ERR!`).
- **`src/values.js`** — tagged value model (`num`/`text`/`bool`/`err`) plus arithmetic/boolean coercion and the cross-kind comparison ordering (number < text < boolean).
- **`src/literal.js`** — literal-cell parsing (empty→0, numeric, the six error tokens, else text).
- **`src/format.js`** — 10-significant-digit rounding and value stringification.
- **`src/sheet.js`** — line splitting/trimming per the exact whitespace rules, address validation, duplicate detection, both raising `SheetError` with the right line number.
- **`src/evaluator.js`** — memoized recursive evaluator with cycle detection via an in-progress marker (yields `#CYCLE!` on self-reference, direct or indirect), operator/function error-propagation rules (left-wins for operators, first-left-to-right-including-ranges wins for functions), `IF`'s lazy branch evaluation, and a separate pure-syntax `collectDeps` walk for the `deps` mode (independent of evaluation, includes both `IF` branches, expands ranges, only keeps addressable cells).
- **`src/cli.js`** — wires it together: validates `argv`, reads all of stdin, reports sheet errors, and prints sorted `values`/`deps` output.

I verified behavior against many spec corners beyond the visible tests (unary/power precedence like `-2^2=4` and `2^3^2=512`, cross-kind and same-kind comparisons, out-of-range addresses (`FOO`, `AAA1`, `A0`, `A1000`) yielding `#REF!` in formulas but a hard error when used as a declaration address, misplaced ranges causing `#ERR!` while direct-argument ranges work, `IF` branch laziness hiding errors/cycles in the untaken branch, wrong-arity calls, `COUNT` ignoring text/bool but still deferring to any error present, case-insensitive/duplicate address handling, and literal `"TRUE"` being text rather than a boolean). ## Self-review summary

I audited the specification sentence by sentence, deriving the exact requirement from each sentence in isolation and testing the smallest input that exercises it, checking exit code, stdout, and stderr byte-for-byte:

- **Usage validation**: 0 args, 2 args, and a wrong word all give exit 2, `error: usage: cli.js values|deps`, nothing on stdout. ✓
- **Line splitting / trailing newline**: no trailing newline, one trailing newline, and a blank final line before a trailing newline all parse correctly with exit 0. ✓
- **Leading-whitespace stripping, blank/`#` lines ignored** (including a tab before `#`). ✓
- **Address/content split**: one run of tabs+spaces skipped, verbatim internal spaces preserved in content. ✓
- **Address shape**: `Z1`, `AA1`, `ZZ999` accepted; `AAA1`, `A1000`, `A0`, `1A`, `A` all rejected with exit 2 and the exact `invalid cell address <ADDR>` message, uppercased even when the input was lowercase (`aaa1`→`AAA1`). ✓
- **Literal parsing**: `-0`→0, `01`→1, `.5`/`1.`/`1.5.5`/`1e5` all correctly fall through to text (no sign-less-decimal, no exponent, no malformed numbers accepted as numbers). ✓
- **Precedence/associativity**: `10-2-3=5`, `100/10/2=5` (left-assoc), `-2^2=4`, `2^3^2=512`, unary `+` works, spaces-anywhere and case-insensitive function names (`sum ( 1 , 2 )`) parse. ✓
- **Grammar rejection** (`=1 2`) → `#ERR!`, exit 0 (sheet still "parses" for CLI purposes). ✓
- **Non-finite results** (huge power, NaN from fractional root of negative) → `#DIV/0!`. ✓
- **Functions**: SUM/MIN/MAX/AVG/COUNT over ranges (including reversed-corner ranges), ABS, IF, wrong arity → `#ERR!`, unknown name → `#NAME?`. ✓
- **Error propagation**: left-operand-wins for operators, first-error-left-to-right-wins for functions (even overriding `COUNT`'s counting, and even when the "error" is an out-of-range bare-word address). ✓
- **`deps`**: dedupes, orders by column then row, includes cells named by "misplaced" (semantically odd but grammatically fine) ranges like `ABS(A1:B2)`, excludes non-addressable bare words (`FOO`), and emits nothing for a literal or a grammar-rejected formula. ✓
- **IF laziness**: the untaken branch's error/cycle is genuinely invisible. ✓
- **Cross-kind/same-kind comparisons**, boolean/number coercion in arithmetic vs. condition position. ✓
- **Empty sheet** produces zero bytes of output for both modes, exit 0. ✓
- **Failure-stops-at-first**: with two faults present, only the earlier line's error is reported and stdout is empty. ✓

No discrepancies were found during this audit, so no code changes were needed. The visible suite (`node --test test/*.test.js`) still passes all 18 tests, and `node_modules` remains absent.

`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It reads a build graph from standard input and takes one of three argument forms: `waves`, `explain`, or `pack` followed by a worker count. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace.

A `task <name> <cost>` line declares a task. A name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. A cost is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without separators, so `01` is the cost 1. A `dep <name> <dependency>...` line makes the first name depend on every later name on the line; a repeated edge counts once, and a `dep` line may appear before the tasks it names. Every name a `dep` line uses must be declared by some `task` line somewhere in the input. An empty input is a valid graph with no task.

`waves` prints one line per wave, `wave K: ` followed by the wave's task names in ascending order separated by single spaces, and then a final line `total T`. Wave 0 holds every task with no dependency and wave K holds every task whose deepest dependency is in wave K-1. `T` is the makespan with unlimited workers: the greatest finish time, or 0 when there is no task. A task's start is the greatest finish of its dependencies, or 0 when it has none, and its finish is its start plus its cost.

`explain` prints one line per task in ascending name order, `<name> start=<s> finish=<f> depth=<d>`, where the start and finish are the ones above and the depth is the wave the task sits in, and then the same final `total T` line.

`pack <workers>` simulates the same graph on that many workers. Time starts at 0. While a worker is free at the current instant and some task is ready, meaning every one of its dependencies has already finished at or before that instant, take the ready task with the greatest priority, breaking ties by ascending name, and start it on the free worker with the smallest index. A task's priority is the cost of the longest chain that begins at it, counting its own cost and then the costs down to any task that nothing depends on. A task of cost 0 finishes at the instant it starts, so its worker is free again at once and its dependents may start in the same instant. When nothing more can start, time advances to the next instant at which a worker becomes free, and the loop repeats. The output is one line per worker in index order, `worker <i>:` followed by ` <name>@<start>-<finish>` for each task it ran in the order it ran them, and then a final line `makespan M` holding the greatest finish, or 0 when there is no task.

A cycle makes the graph unschedulable: write `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exit 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task.

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It reads a build graph from standard input and takes one of three argument forms: `waves`, `explain`, or `pack` followed by a worker count. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace.

A `task <name> <cost>` line declares a task. A name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. A cost is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without separators, so `01` is the cost 1. A `dep <name> <dependency>...` line makes the first name depend on every later name on the line; a repeated edge counts once, and a `dep` line may appear before the tasks it names. Every name a `dep` line uses must be declared by some `task` line somewhere in the input. An empty input is a valid graph with no task.

`waves` prints one line per wave, `wave K: ` followed by the wave's task names in ascending order separated by single spaces, and then a final line `total T`. Wave 0 holds every task with no dependency and wave K holds every task whose deepest dependency is in wave K-1. `T` is the makespan with unlimited workers: the greatest finish time, or 0 when there is no task. A task's start is the greatest finish of its dependencies, or 0 when it has none, and its finish is its start plus its cost.

`explain` prints one line per task in ascending name order, `<name> start=<s> finish=<f> depth=<d>`, where the start and finish are the ones above and the depth is the wave the task sits in, and then the same final `total T` line.

`pack <workers>` simulates the same graph on that many workers. Time starts at 0. While a worker is free at the current instant and some task is ready, meaning every one of its dependencies has already finished at or before that instant, take the ready task with the greatest priority, breaking ties by ascending name, and start it on the free worker with the smallest index. A task's priority is the cost of the longest chain that begins at it, counting its own cost and then the costs down to any task that nothing depends on. `taskrun` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/taskrun.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.

Two directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.

`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.

`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.

`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.

A task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. The first watched path with a reason decides that the task runs, and the reason is `new <path>` when the snapshot records no digest for it, `missing <path>` when the snapshot records one but the workspace has no such file, and `changed <path>` when the file's digest differs from the recorded one; a file whose digest matches gives no reason. A task no watched path condemns runs anyway when some dependency runs, with the reason `needs <dep>` naming the lexicographically smallest dependency that runs, so a path reason always wins over a dependency one. `plan` prints one line per task in the order `order` prints, `run <name> <reason>` or `skip <name>`, and then a final line `total run=<r> skip=<s>` counting the two. # taskrun

A dependency-aware task runner with no dependencies of its own. It reads a task file from standard input and answers questions about it; it never executes a command.

## Layout

| File | What it owns |
| --- | --- |
| `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
| `src/parse.js` | the task-file grammar and the refusals it words, as `ParseError` |
| `src/graph.js` | run order over the dependency edges |
| `src/digest.js` | the FNV-1a digest the snapshot format records |

`test/taskrun.test.js` is the suite for what is already here. `data/files/` holds the workspace files the examples name, and `data/snapshots/` the digest snapshots.

## The task file

One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace.

```
# build.tasks
task build node build.js
task bundle node bundle.js
needs bundle build
```

`task <name> <word>...` declares a task whose command is the remaining words joined with single spaces. `needs <name> <dependency>...` adds dependencies; a repeated edge counts once, and a `needs` line may stand before the `task` line it names.

## Modes

- `order` prints the task names one per line, in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose dependencies have all been printed.
- `show <name>` prints `<name>: <command>` and then `needs: ` followed by the dependencies in ascending order, or `-` when there are none.
- `digest <path>...` prints `<path> <digest>` for each path in argument order, with `missing` in place of a digest for a path that is not there. The digest is 32-bit FNV-1a over the file's bytes — offset basis `0x811c9dc5`, prime `16777619`, xor then multiply — as eight lowercase hex digits.

## Failures

Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A parse failure names its 1-based input line: `error: line 2: unknown directive run`. The messages are `expected task <name> <word>...`, `expected needs <name> <dependency>...`, `invalid task name <name>`, `task <name> is declared twice` and `unknown directive <word>`. A `needs` line naming a task no `task` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown task <name>`, and so is `show` on such a name.

## Known gaps

`order` does not detect a dependency cycle: it stops as soon as nothing is ready and leaves every task in the cycle out of its output. The task file has no way to declare which files a task reads or writes, so nothing here can tell whether a task is up to date.

1: /** The task-file parser: directives to tasks, with the failures the specification words. */
2: 
3: const NAME = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: 
5: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line it was read from, or 0 when it names none. */
6: export class ParseError extends Error {
7:   /**
8:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names no line.
9:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the `error: ` prefix.
10:    */
11:   constructor(line, message) {
12:     super(message)
13:     this.name = 'ParseError'
14:     this.line = line
15:   }
16: }
17: 
18: /** Whether a word is a usable task name. */
19: function isName(word) {
20:   return NAME.test(word)
21: }
22: 
23: /**
24:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
25:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
26:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
27:  */
28: export function splitLines(text) {
29:   const split = text.split('\n')
30:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
31:   return split
32: }
33: 
34: /**
35:  * Parse a task file into its tasks.
36:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
37:  * @returns {Map<string, {name: string, command: string, needs: string[]}>} the tasks by name, in declaration order.
38:  */
39: export function parse(lines) {
40:   const tasks = new Map()
41:   const referenced = []
42:   const attachments = []
43:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
44:     const line = index + 1
45:     const text = raw.trim()
46:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
47:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
48:     if (words[0] === 'task') {
49:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, 'expected task <name> <word>...')
50:       const name = words[1]
51:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
52:       if (tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `task ${name} is declared twice`)
53:       tasks.set(name, { name, command: words.slice(2).join(' '), needs: [] })
54:     } else if (words[0] === 'needs') {
55:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, 'expected needs <name> <dependency>...')
56:       const [, name, ...values] = words
57:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
58:       referenced.push(name)
59:       for (const value of values) {
60:         if (!isName(value)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${value}`)
61:         referenced.push(value)
62:       }
63:       attachments.push({ name, values })
64:     } else {
65:       throw new ParseError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
66:     }
67:   }
68:   for (const name of referenced) {
69:     if (!tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(0, `unknown task ${name}`)
70:   }
71:   for (const { name, values } of attachments) {
72:     const list = tasks.get(name).needs
73:     for (const value of values) {
74:       if (!list.includes(value)) list.push(value)
75:     }
76:   }
77:   return tasks
78: }

1: /** Ordering the task graph. */
2: 
3: /**
4:  * The tasks in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose
5:  * dependencies have all been emitted. A cycle has no such task, so the order
6:  * stops early and leaves the tasks in it out.
7:  * @param {Map<string, {needs: string[]}>} tasks - the parsed tasks.
8:  * @returns {string[]} the names in run order.
9:  */
10: export function order(tasks) {
11:   const remaining = new Set(tasks.keys())
12:   const emitted = new Set()
13:   const out = []
14:   while (remaining.size > 0) {
15:     const ready = [...remaining].filter(name => tasks.get(name).needs.every(need => emitted.has(need))).sort()
16:     if (ready.length === 0) break
17:     remaining.delete(ready[0])
18:     emitted.add(ready[0])
19:     out.push(ready[0])
20:   }
21:   return out
22: }

1: #!/usr/bin/env node
2: /** The command: `order`, `show <name>` and `digest <path>...`. */
3: 
4: import { existsSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
5: import { digestBytes } from './digest.js'
6: import { order } from './graph.js'
7: import { parse, ParseError, splitLines } from './parse.js'
8: 
9: const USAGE = 'usage: cli.js order|show <name>|digest <path>...'
10: 
11: /** Report one failure the way the specification words it, and stop. */
12: function fail(message, code = 2) {
13:   process.stderr.write(`error: ${message}\n`)
14:   process.exit(code)
15: }
16: 
17: /** One `show` field, with `-` standing for an empty list. */
18: function field(label, values) {
19:   return `${label}: ${values.length === 0 ? '-' : [...values].sort().join(' ')}`
20: }
21: 
22: const argv = process.argv.slice(2)
23: const mode = argv[0]
24: const arity = { order: 1, show: 2 }
25: if (mode === 'digest' ? argv.length < 2 : argv.length !== arity[mode]) fail(USAGE)
26: 
27: let tasks
28: try {
29:   tasks = parse(splitLines(readFileSync(0, 'utf8')))
30: } catch (error) {
31:   if (!(error instanceof ParseError)) throw error
32:   fail(error.line === 0 ? error.message : `line ${error.line}: ${error.message}`)
33: }
34: 
35: const out = []
36: if (mode === 'order') {
37:   for (const name of order(tasks)) out.push(name)
38: } else if (mode === 'show') {
39:   const task = tasks.get(argv[1])
40:   if (task === undefined) fail(`unknown task ${argv[1]}`)
41:   out.push(`${task.name}: ${task.command}`)
42:   out.push(field('needs', task.needs))
43: } else {
44:   for (const path of argv.slice(1)) {
45:     out.push(`${path} ${existsSync(path) ? digestBytes(readFileSync(path)) : 'missing'}`)
46:   }
47: }
48: process.stdout.write(out.map(line => `${line}\n`).join(''))

1: /** FNV-1a over raw bytes, the digest the snapshot format records. */
2: 
3: const OFFSET = 0x811c9dc5
4: const PRIME = 16777619
5: 
6: /**
7:  * The 32-bit FNV-1a digest of a byte buffer as eight lowercase hex digits.
8:  * @param {Buffer} bytes - the bytes to digest.
9:  * @returns {string} the digest.
10:  */
11: export function digestBytes(bytes) {
12:   let hash = OFFSET >>> 0
13:   for (const byte of bytes) {
14:     hash = (hash ^ byte) >>> 0
15:     hash = Math.imul(hash, PRIME) >>> 0
16:   }
17:   return hash.toString(16).padStart(8, '0')
18: }

  "prompt": "`taskrun` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/taskrun.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.\n\nTwo directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.\n\n`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.\n\n`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.\n\n`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.\n\nA task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. `taskrun` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/taskrun.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.

Two directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.

`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.

`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.

`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.

A task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. The first watched path with a reason decides that the task runs, and the reason is `new <path>` when the snapshot records no digest for it, `missing <path>` when the snapshot records one but the workspace has no such file, and `changed <path>` when the file's digest differs from the recorded one; a file whose digest matches gives no reason. A task no watched path condemns runs anyway when some dependency runs, with the reason `needs <dep>` naming the lexicographically smallest dependency that runs, so a path reason always wins over a dependency one. `plan` prints one line per task in the order `order` prints, `run <name> <reason>` or `skip <name>`, and then a final line `total run=<r> skip=<s>` counting the two. `src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `normalize` or `resolve`, reads UTF-8 text from standard input, and writes one result line per input line to standard output. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every remaining line is a record, including an empty one. Exit 0 when every record succeeds.

In `normalize` mode each record is one URI reference and its output line is the normalized form. In `resolve` mode each record is a base URI, one space, and a reference; the output line is the reference resolved against the base and then normalized. The first space separates the two, so a reference may contain spaces and a base may not.

Parse a URI reference into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by RFC 3986's generic syntax: an optional scheme running to the first `:`, which may not be preceded by any `/`, `?` or `#`; an optional authority introduced by `//` and running to the next `/`, `?` or `#`; the path up to the next `?` or `#`; an optional query from `?` to the next `#`; an optional fragment from `#` to the end. An absent component and an empty one are different, so `http://a/b?` has an empty query, `http://a/b` has none, and both print back the way they came. Inside an authority the userinfo is everything before the last `@`, the port is everything after the first `:` that follows the last `]`, and the host is what lies between.

Normalization applies in this order. Lowercase the scheme, using ASCII rules only. Normalize percent-encodings in every component: uppercase the two hexadecimal digits of each `%XX`, then replace the triplet with the character it encodes when that character is unreserved, meaning one of `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `-`, `.`, `_` and `~`. Lowercase the host, using ASCII rules only and leaving the userinfo alone. Drop the port when it is written empty or written with exactly the digits of the scheme's default, which is 80 for `http` and `ws`, 443 for `https` and `wss`, and 21 for `ftp`; no other scheme has one, and a port padded with a leading zero is not written with those digits and stays. Remove dot segments from the path by RFC 3986 section 5.2.4, so a `.` segment disappears, a `..` segment removes the segment before it, and a `..` that would climb above the root is discarded. Finally, when an authority is present and the path is empty, make the path `/`. Dot removal never touches the query or the fragment.

Resolve by RFC 3986 section 5.2.2 in its strict form, in which a reference that repeats the base's scheme is still an absolute URI. A reference that writes a scheme is itself the target, with the dot segments removed from its path. A reference that writes an authority takes the base's scheme and keeps everything else of its own. A reference with neither and an empty path takes the base's authority and path, takes the base's query only when it writes no query of its own, and takes its own fragment, which may be absent. Otherwise, when the reference's path does not start with `/`, merge it onto the base's: keep everything of the base path up to and including its last `/`, or use the reference path alone when the base path holds no `/`, except that a base that has an authority and an empty path contributes a single leading `/`. Remove the dot segments from the resulting path, take the base's authority and the reference's query and fragment, and normalize the whole.
