goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `normalize` or `resolve`, reads UTF-8 text from standard input, and writes one result line per input line to standard output. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every remaining line is a record, including an empty one. Exit 0 when every record succeeds.

In `normalize` mode each record is one URI reference and its output line is the normalized form. In `resolve` mode each record is a base URI, one space, and a reference; the output line is the reference resolved against the base and then normalized. The first space separates the two, so a reference may contain spaces and a base may not.

Parse a URI reference into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by RFC 3986's generic syntax: an optional scheme running to the first `:`, which may not be preceded by any `/`, `?` or `#`; an optional authority introduced by `//` and running to the next `/`, `?` or `#`; the path up to the next `?` or `#`; an optional query from `?` to the next `#`; an optional fragment from `#` to the end. An absent component and an empty one are different, so `http://a/b?` has an empty query, `http://a/b` has none, and both print back the way they came. Inside an authority the userinfo is everything before the last `@`, the port is everything after the first `:` that follows the last `]`, and the host is what lies between.

Normalization applies in this order. Lowercase the scheme, using ASCII rules only. Normalize percent-encodings in every component: uppercase the two hexadecimal digits of each `%XX`, then replace the triplet with the character it encodes when that character is unreserved, meaning one of `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `-`, `.`, `_` and `~`. Lowercase the host, using ASCII rules only and leaving the userinfo alone. Drop the port when it is written empty or written with exactly the digits of the scheme's default, which is 80 for `http` and `ws`, 443 for `https` and `wss`, and 21 for `ftp`; no other scheme has one, and a port padded with a leading zero is not written with those digits and stays. Remove dot segments from the path by RFC 3986 section 5.2.4, so a `.` segment disappears, a `..` segment removes the segment before it, and a `..` that would climb above the root is discarded. Finally, when an authority is present and the path is empty, make the path `/`. Dot removal never touches the query or the fragment.

Resolve by RFC 3986 section 5.2.2 in its strict form, in which a reference that repeats the base's scheme is still an absolute URI. A reference that writes a scheme is itself the target, with the dot segments removed from its path. A reference that writes an authority takes the base's scheme and keeps everything else of its own. A reference with neither and an empty path takes the base's authority and path, takes the base's query only when it writes no query of its own, and takes its own fragment, which may be absent. Otherwise, when the reference's path does not start with `/`, merge it onto the base's: keep everything of the base path up to and including its last `/`, or use the reference path alone when the base path holds no `/`, except that a base that has an authority and an empty path contributes a single leading `/`. Remove the dot segments from the resulting path, take the base's authority and the reference's query and fragment, and normalize the whole.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js normalize|resolve` when the arguments are not exactly one of the two mode words; `error: line N: expected a base and a reference` when a `resolve` record holds no space; `error: line N: the base has no scheme` when the base of a `resolve` record writes no scheme; and `error: line N: the path has a truncated percent-encoding` when a `%` is not followed by two hexadecimal digits, with `path` replaced by `userinfo`, `host`, `query` or `fragment` for whichever component carries it, those five being checked in that order. A line beginning with `[` is a header. `[name]` makes that table current, creating the tables on the way; when the name already holds anything other than a table the reason is `<path> is not a table`, and otherwise a table a header already made current may not be named by a second `[name]` header, though a table that only came into being on the way to a deeper one, or from a dotted key, still may. `[[name]]` appends a fresh table to the array of tables at that name, creating it when it is absent, and makes that fresh table current; when the name already holds anything other than an array of tables the reason is `<path> is not an array of tables`. Walking through an array of tables uses its last element. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the closing bracket is an error.

Every other line is `<dotted name> = <value>`, assigning inside the current table, creating the tables the dots walk through. A name already holding anything may not be assigned again, and a dot may not walk through a name that holds something other than a table or an array of tables.

A value is one of: `true` or `false`; an integer, an optional `+` or `-` and runs of digits joined by single `_`; a float, an integer with a fraction of `.` and digit runs, an exponent of `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digit runs, or both; a basic string in double quotes carrying the escapes `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\0` and `\uXXXX` with exactly four hexadecimal digits; a literal string in single quotes carrying no escapes; an array of values in `[` and `]`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing one trailing comma; or an inline table of `<dotted name> = <value>` pairs in `{` and `}`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing no trailing comma. Arrays and inline tables may hold each other. A bare word that is none of these is an error naming that word, while a value required but never written, because the line ends or a `,`, a `]` or a `}` comes first, is `expected a value`. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the value is an error.

`json` prints the document as JSON indented by two spaces, with the members of every object in ascending key order by code point, and a trailing newline; an array of tables prints as a JSON array, and a float prints however JSON prints its number, so a float that happens to be whole prints without a fraction. `keys` instead prints one line per node below the root, `<path> <type>`, walking objects in ascending key order and arrays in index order, depth first, each node before its children. A path joins object keys with `.` and appends `[i]` for an array index, using the key text as written after decoding. The type is `table`, `array`, `string`, `integer`, `float` or `boolean`, and an array of tables is an `array`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The message is `error: usage: cli.js json|keys` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: line N: <reason>` where the reason is one of `expected a name`, `expected a value`, `expected key = value`, `expected = in an inline table`, `unterminated string`, `unterminated array`, `unterminated inline table`, `unterminated table header`, `invalid escape \<character>`, `invalid value <text>`, `trailing text after a value`, `trailing text after a table header`, `key <path> is defined twice` with the path counted from the root, `table <path> is defined twice`, `<path> is not a table`, and `<path> is not an array of tables`. `conflayers` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/conflayers.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the two layered modes its `merge` primitive was built for, make the declared types real, and report a bad value where it was written. Everything `README.md` documents about `dump`, `get`, the INI grammar and the existing failures stays exactly as it is, including every message and every column; the work spans the parser, the schema, the layer stack, and the command.

`load <base> <site>` and `origin <base> <site>` each stack three layers, weakest first: the INI file named by the first argument, the INI file named by the second, and an environment layer read from standard input. A later layer overrides a key an earlier one set, one key at a time, so a file that sets only `server.port` leaves every other key to the layer below it. The layers are read in that order, and a layer's failures are all reported before the next layer is read.

The environment layer is a line per variable. A line is trimmed first; an empty one, and one beginning with `#`, is ignored. The rest is `NAME=VALUE`: the text before the first `=` is the name, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A setting travels under `CONF_` followed by its key uppercased with every `.` replaced by `_`, so `server.port` arrives as `CONF_SERVER_PORT`. Its failures carry a position too, worded `error: <stdin>:<line>:<column>: ` followed by `expected NAME=VALUE` or `expected a variable name` or `unknown environment variable <NAME>` or `<NAME> is set twice`, each reported at the line's first non-space character and each counting columns the way the INI parser does.

Both modes are strict about keys where `dump` is lenient: a key an INI layer sets and the schema does not know fails with `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: unknown setting <key>` at the value's position, and a layer's keys are checked in the order the file writes them, after that file parses. The value's position is the column of its first character, or, when the value is empty, one past the line's last non-space character.

`origin <base> <site>` prints `<key> <layer>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the layer is `base`, `site`, `env`, or `default` when no layer set the key.

`load <base> <site>` prints `<key>=<value>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the value is the winning layer's text coerced by the key's declared type, or the schema default coerced the same way. A `string` is its text. An `integer` is an optional `-` and then digits without a leading zero, unless the number is exactly `0`, and renders as written. A `boolean` is `true` or `false`, lowercase, and renders as written. An `enum` is one of its declared members and renders as written. A `duration` is digits followed by `ms`, `s`, `m` or `h`, and renders as its whole number of milliseconds. A `list` is items separated by commas, each trimmed, with a repeat dropped and the order kept, rendered joined by single commas; empty text is the empty list and renders empty, but an empty item between two commas is a failure. A value that does not fit its type fails with `error: <where>: <message>`, where `<where>` is the file and position it was written at, or `<stdin>` and its position when the environment layer set it, and the message is `<key> is not an integer: <text>`, `<key> is not a boolean: <text>`, `<key> is not one of <members joined by |>: <text>`, `<key> is not a duration: <text>` or `<key> has an empty item: <text>`. The keys are coerced in ascending order, so the first failing key in that order decides.

1: # conflayers
2: 
3: A configuration loader with no dependencies. It reads INI files, knows a fixed schema of settings, and answers what one of them is set to.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/ini.js` | the INI grammar and the refusals it words, as `IniError`, each with a line and a column |
11: | `src/schema.js` | `SETTINGS`, the known settings with their declared type and default text |
12: | `src/layer.js` | `merge`, which stacks layers so that the last one to set a key wins |
13: 
14: `test/conflayers.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the INI files the examples name.
15: 
16: ## The INI grammar
17: 
18: A line is trimmed first. An empty one, and one beginning with `#` or `;`, is ignored. `[name]` opens a section, and a section may be opened more than once. Anything else is `key = value`: the text before the first `=` is the key, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A key outside a section keeps its own name; a key inside one is prefixed with the section name and a dot, so `port` under `[server]` is `server.port`. A name and a key are one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. Nothing inside a value is special: `#` and `;` open a comment only at the start of a line.
19: 
20: ```ini
21: log.file = /var/log/app.log
22: 
23: [server]
24: port = 9090
25: ```
26: 
27: ## The schema
28: 
29: | Key | Type | Default |
30: | --- | --- | --- |
31: | `log.file` | string | (empty) |
32: | `log.level` | enum `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` | `info` |
33: | `log.rotate` | boolean | `true` |
34: | `retry.attempts` | integer | `3` |
35: | `retry.backoff` | duration | `250ms` |
36: | `server.host` | string | `localhost` |
37: | `server.port` | integer | `8080` |
38: | `server.timeout` | duration | `30s` |
39: | `server.tls` | boolean | `false` |
40: | `tags` | list | (empty) |
41: 
42: The types are declared but nothing here enforces them yet: every mode below prints the raw text as the file wrote it.
43: 
44: ## Modes
45: 
46: - `dump <file>` prints `<key>=<raw text>` for every schema key in ascending order, falling back to the schema default for a key the file leaves out. A key the schema does not know is ignored.
47: - `get <file> <key>` prints the raw text of one setting, or its default. A key outside the schema is refused.
48: 
49: ## Failures
50: 
51: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure carries the position it was read at, as `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: <message>`, where the column counts characters of the raw line from 1, leading whitespace included. The messages are `expected "]"`, reported one past the line's last non-space character; `expected a section name` and `invalid section name <name>`, at the name's first character; `expected a section header or key = value` and `invalid key <key>`, at the line's first non-space character; `expected a key`, at the `=`; and `key <key> is set twice`, at the line's first non-space character. A file that cannot be read is refused as `error: cannot read <path>`, an unknown key as `error: unknown setting <key>`, and a malformed argument list with the usage line.
52: 
53: ## Known gaps
54: 
55: Only one file is ever read, so the `merge` primitive stacks a single layer and nothing overrides anything. Nothing reads the environment. The declared types do nothing: `server.port = eighty` loads as happily as `server.port = 80`, and a caller has to coerce the text itself. `IniError` carries a position, but the parse result does not, so nothing downstream could say where a bad value was written.

1: /** The INI reader: dotted keys and the raw text of each value. */
2: 
3: const NAME = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: 
5: /** One refusal of an INI line, carrying the 1-based line and column it was read at. */
6: export class IniError extends Error {
7:   /**
8:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line.
9:    * @param {number} column - the 1-based column of the raw line.
10:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
11:    */
12:   constructor(line, column, message) {
13:     super(message)
14:     this.name = 'IniError'
15:     this.line = line
16:     this.column = column
17:   }
18: }
19: 
20: /** The 1-based column of the first non-space character of `raw`. */
21: function indent(raw) {
22:   return raw.length - raw.trimStart().length + 1
23: }
24: 
25: /**
26:  * Parse INI text into its settings.
27:  * @param {string} text - the file's whole text.
28:  * @returns {Map<string, string>} each dotted key's raw value, in the order the file writes them.
29:  * @throws {IniError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
30:  */
31: export function parse(text) {
32:   const lines = text.split('\n')
33:   if (lines.length > 0 && lines[lines.length - 1] === '') lines.pop()
34:   const values = new Map()
35:   let section = ''
36:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
37:     const line = index + 1
38:     const trimmed = raw.trim()
39:     if (trimmed === '' || trimmed.startsWith('#') || trimmed.startsWith(';')) continue
40:     if (trimmed.startsWith('[')) {
41:       if (!trimmed.endsWith(']')) throw new IniError(line, raw.trimEnd().length + 1, 'expected "]"')
42:       const name = trimmed.slice(1, -1)
43:       if (name === '') throw new IniError(line, indent(raw) + 1, 'expected a section name')
44:       if (!NAME.test(name)) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw) + 1, `invalid section name ${name}`)
45:       section = name
46:       continue
47:     }
48:     const split = trimmed.indexOf('=')
49:     if (split === -1) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw), 'expected a section header or key = value')
50:     const key = trimmed.slice(0, split).trim()
51:     if (key === '') throw new IniError(line, indent(raw) + split, 'expected a key')
52:     if (!NAME.test(key)) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw), `invalid key ${key}`)
53:     const full = section === '' ? key : `${section}.${key}`
54:     if (values.has(full)) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw), `key ${full} is set twice`)
55:     values.set(full, trimmed.slice(split + 1).trim())
56:   }
57:   return values
58: }

## Summary

I implemented `load` and `origin` modes for `conflayers`, made the schema types real, and threaded value positions through the parser, changing only files under `src/`:

- **`src/ini.js`**: `parse` now returns `Map<key, {text, line, column}>` instead of plain strings — `column` is the value's own position (its first character, or one past the line's last non-space character when empty), computed with the same column-counting rules as the existing grammar errors. All existing `IniError` messages/positions are untouched.

- **`src/env.js`** (new): parses the stdin environment layer — trims lines, skips blanks/`#` comments, splits `NAME=VALUE`, maps `CONF_*` names back to schema keys, and reports `expected NAME=VALUE`, `expected a variable name`, `unknown environment variable <NAME>`, or `<NAME> is set twice`, each at the line's first non-space character, plus a value position computed the same way as the INI parser's.

- **`src/schema.js`**: added `coerce(declared, text)`, implementing the six types (`string`, `integer`, `boolean`, `enum`, `duration`, `list`) exactly as specified — including the leading-zero integer rule, `ms/s/m/h`→milliseconds duration rendering via `BigInt` (no precision loss), and list dedup/empty-item detection — throwing the exact `<key> is not ...: <text>` / `<key> has an empty item: <text>` messages.

- **`src/layer.js`**: `merge` now tags each merged entry with the name of the layer that won it (`base`/`site`/`env`/the caller's own label), preserving `text`/`line`/`column`.

- **`src/cli.js`**: added `load <base> <site>` and `origin <base> <site>`, each stacking base → site → env (stdin), checking each INI layer's keys against the schema immediately after it parses (in file order), then either printing `<key> <layer-or-default>` (origin) or coercing each key in ascending order and printing `<key>=<value>` — failing on the first miscoercion at the position (`<file>` or `<stdin>`) it was written at. `dump`/`get` behavior and the usage line (now naming all four forms) are otherwise preserved.

goal.objective:
`conflayers` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/conflayers.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the two layered modes its `merge` primitive was built for, make the declared types real, and report a bad value where it was written. Everything `README.md` documents about `dump`, `get`, the INI grammar and the existing failures stays exactly as it is, including every message and every column; the work spans the parser, the schema, the layer stack, and the command.

`load <base> <site>` and `origin <base> <site>` each stack three layers, weakest first: the INI file named by the first argument, the INI file named by the second, and an environment layer read from standard input. A later layer overrides a key an earlier one set, one key at a time, so a file that sets only `server.port` leaves every other key to the layer below it. The layers are read in that order, and a layer's failures are all reported before the next layer is read.

The environment layer is a line per variable. A line is trimmed first; an empty one, and one beginning with `#`, is ignored. The rest is `NAME=VALUE`: the text before the first `=` is the name, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A setting travels under `CONF_` followed by its key uppercased with every `.` replaced by `_`, so `server.port` arrives as `CONF_SERVER_PORT`. goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `normalize` or `resolve`, reads UTF-8 text from standard input, and writes one result line per input line to standard output. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every remaining line is a record, including an empty one. Exit 0 when every record succeeds.

In `normalize` mode each record is one URI reference and its output line is the normalized form. In `resolve` mode each record is a base URI, one space, and a reference; the output line is the reference resolved against the base and then normalized. The first space separates the two, so a reference may contain spaces and a base may not.

Parse a URI reference into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by RFC 3986's generic syntax: an optional scheme running to the first `:`, which may not be preceded by any `/`, `?` or `#`; an optional authority introduced by `//` and running to the next `/`, `?` or `#`; the path up to the next `?` or `#`; an optional query from `?` to the next `#`; an optional fragment from `#` to the end. An absent component and an empty one are different, so `http://a/b?` has an empty query, `http://a/b` has none, and both print back the way they came. Inside an authority the userinfo is everything before the last `@`, the port is everything after the first `:` that follows the last `]`, and the host is what lies between.

Normalization applies in this order. Lowercase the scheme, using ASCII rules only. Normalize percent-encodings in every component: uppercase the two hexadecimal digits of each `%XX`, then replace the triplet with the character it encodes when that character is unreserved, meaning one of `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `-`, `.`, `_` and `~`. Lowercase the host, using ASCII rules only and leaving the userinfo alone. Drop the port when it is written empty or written with exactly the digits of the scheme's default, which is 80 for `http` and `ws`, 443 for `https` and `wss`, and 21 for `ftp`; no other scheme has one, and a port padded with a leading zero is not written with those digits and stays. Remove dot segments from the path by RFC 3986 section 5.2.4, so a `.` segment disappears, a `..` segment removes the segment before it, and a `..` that would climb above the root is discarded. Finally, when an authority is present and the path is empty, make the path `/`. Dot removal never touches the query or the fragment.

Resolve by RFC 3986 section 5.2.2 in its strict form, in which a reference that repeats the base's scheme is still an absolute URI. A reference that writes a scheme is itself the target, with the dot segments removed from its path. A reference that writes an authority takes the base's scheme and keeps everything else of its own. A reference with neither and an empty path takes the base's authority and path, takes the base's query only when it writes no query of its own, and takes its own fragment, which may be absent. Otherwise, when the reference's path does not start with `/`, merge it onto the base's: keep everything of the base path up to and including its last `/`, or use the reference path alone when the base path holds no `/`, except that a base that has an authority and an empty path contributes a single leading `/`. Remove the dot segments from the resulting path, take the base's authority and the reference's query and fragment, and normalize the whole.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js normalize|resolve` when the arguments are not exactly one of the two mode words; `error: line N: expected a base and a reference` when a `resolve` record holds no space; `error: line N: the base has no scheme` when the base of a `resolve` record writes no scheme; and `error: line N: the path has a truncated percent-encoding` when a `%` is not followed by two hexadecimal digits, with `path` replaced by `userinfo`, `host`, `query` or `fragment` for whichever component carries it, those five being checked in that order. N counts records from 1. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. 1: # jobq
2: 
3: A job-queue simulator with no dependencies. It reads a log from standard input and replays it on one worker against a clock that only moves when the simulation asks it to, so a run is the same on every machine and in every order.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/parse.js` | the log grammar and the refusals it words, as `LogError` |
11: | `src/queue.js` | the simulation: what starts when, and what the rate limit holds back |
12: | `src/clock.js` | `createClock`, the monotonic clock the simulation advances by hand |
13: 
14: `test/jobq.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the policy files the examples name.
15: 
16: ## The log
17: 
18: One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace. Every number is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign or a separator.
19: 
20: ```
21: limit 2 10
22: job build 5 ok
23: job flaky 3 fail ok
24: submit 0 build
25: submit 0 flaky
26: ```
27: 
28: `limit <starts> <window>` allows at most `<starts>` starts inside any window of `<window>` milliseconds, and may appear at most once. `job <id> <duration> <outcome>...` declares a job that occupies the worker for `<duration>` milliseconds and whose attempts turn out as the listed `ok` and `fail` words, the last of which repeats. An id is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. `submit <at> <id>` puts a declared job in the queue at that instant; a job may be submitted at most once.
29: 
30: ## The simulation
31: 
32: The clock starts at 0 and one worker runs everything. Take the queued attempt with the smallest ready time, breaking ties by submission order, and advance the clock to that ready time. If a rate limit is in force and the last `<starts>` starts all fall inside the window ending now, advance the clock to the instant the oldest of them leaves it. The attempt starts at the clock's instant and finishes `<duration>` later, and the clock advances to that finish. A job of duration 0 finishes in the instant it starts. A failed attempt is simply over: nothing here retries it.
33: 
34: ## Modes
35: 
36: - `trace` prints one line per attempt in the order the attempts started, `<start> <id> attempt=<n> <outcome> finish=<finish>`, and then a final `end <clock>` line.
37: - `summary` prints one line per submitted job in ascending id order, `<id> attempts=<n> <outcome of its last attempt>`, and then the same final `end <clock>` line.
38: 
39: A declared job nothing submits never runs and appears nowhere.
40: 
41: ## Failures
42: 
43: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure names its 1-based log line: `error: line 2: unknown directive cancel`. The messages are `expected limit <starts> <window>`, `expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...`, `expected submit <at> <id>`, `invalid job id <id>`, `invalid outcome <word>`, `<field> must be a non-negative integer` and `<field> must be a positive integer` naming `at`, `duration`, `starts` or `window`, `job <id> is declared twice`, `job <id> is submitted twice`, `limit is declared twice`, and `unknown directive <word>`. A `submit` line naming a job no `job` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown job <id>`. A malformed argument list is refused with the usage line.
44: 
45: ## Known gaps
46: 
47: A failure is the end of a job: there is no retry, no backoff, and nowhere for a job that never succeeds to go. The rate limit and nothing else can be configured, it can only come from the log itself, and there is no way to run the same log under a different policy.

(End of file - total 47 lines)

1: #!/usr/bin/env node
2: /** The command: `trace` and `summary`, each over the log on standard input. */
3: 
4: import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
5: import { LogError, parse, splitLines } from './parse.js'
6: import { run } from './queue.js'
7: 
8: const USAGE = 'usage: cli.js trace|summary'
9: 
10: /** Report one failure the way the specification words it, and stop. */
11: function fail(message) {
12:   process.stderr.write(`error: ${message}\n`)
13:   process.exit(2)
14: }
15: 
16: const argv = process.argv.slice(2)
17: const mode = argv[0]
18: if (!['trace', 'summary'].includes(mode) || argv.length !== 1) fail(USAGE)
19: 
20: const policy = {}
21: let parsed
22: try {
23:   parsed = parse(splitLines(readFileSync(0, 'utf8')), policy)
24: } catch (error) {
25:   if (!(error instanceof LogError)) throw error
26:   fail(error.line === 0 ? error.message : `line ${error.line}: ${error.message}`)
27: }
28: 
29: const { attempts, end } = run(parsed.jobs, parsed.submissions, policy)
30: const out = []
31: if (mode === 'trace') {
32:   for (const one of attempts) out.push(`${one.start} ${one.id} attempt=${one.attempt} ${one.outcome} finish=${one.finish}`)
33: } else {
34:   for (const { id } of [...parsed.submissions].sort((left, right) => (left.id < right.id ? -1 : 1))) {
35:     const own = attempts.filter(one => one.id === id)
36:     out.push(`${id} attempts=${own.length} ${own[own.length - 1].outcome}`)
37:   }
38: }
39: out.push(`end ${end}`)
40: process.stdout.write(out.map(line => `${line}\n`).join(''))

3: /**
4:  * A clock starting at zero.

6:  */
7: export function createClock() {
8:   let instant = 0
9:   return {
10:     now: () => instant,
11:     advanceTo: (target) => {
12:       if (target > instant) instant = target

14:   }
15: }

1: /** The log grammar: the directives, and the failures each one words. */
2: 
3: const ID = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: const DIGITS = /^[0-9]+$/
5: 
6: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line, or 0 when the failure names none. */
7: export class LogError extends Error {
8:   /**
9:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names no line.
10:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
11:    */
12:   constructor(line, message) {
13:     super(message)
14:     this.name = 'LogError'
15:     this.line = line
16:   }
17: }
18: 
19: /**
20:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
21:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
22:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
23:  */
24: export function splitLines(text) {
25:   const split = text.split('\n')
26:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
27:   return split
28: }
29: 
30: /** One field read as a non-negative integer, or the failure that names it. */
31: function count(line, field, word) {
32:   if (!DIGITS.test(word)) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a non-negative integer`)
33:   return Number(word)
34: }
35: 
36: /** One field read as a positive integer, or the failure that names it. */
37: function positive(line, field, word) {
38:   const value = count(line, field, word)
39:   if (value < 1) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a positive integer`)
40:   return value
41: }
42: 
43: /**
44:  * Parse the job log.
45:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
46:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}}} policy - the policy the log sets, edited in place.
47:  * @returns {{jobs: Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>, submissions: {id: string, at: number}[]}} the declared jobs and the submissions in input order.
48:  * @throws {LogError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
49:  */
50: export function parse(lines, policy) {
51:   const jobs = new Map()
52:   const submissions = []
53:   const submitted = new Map()
54:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
55:     const line = index + 1
56:     const text = raw.trim()
57:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
58:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
59:     if (words[0] === 'limit') {
60:       if (words.length !== 3) throw new LogError(line, 'expected limit <starts> <window>')
61:       if (policy.limit !== undefined) throw new LogError(line, 'limit is declared twice')
62:       policy.limit = { starts: positive(line, 'starts', words[1]), window: positive(line, 'window', words[2]) }
63:     } else if (words[0] === 'job') {
64:       if (words.length < 4) throw new LogError(line, 'expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...')
65:       const id = words[1]
66:       if (!ID.test(id)) throw new LogError(line, `invalid job id ${id}`)
67:       if (jobs.has(id)) throw new LogError(line, `job ${id} is declared twice`)
68:       const duration = count(line, 'duration', words[2])
69:       for (const outcome of words.slice(3)) {
70:         if (outcome !== 'ok' && outcome !== 'fail') throw new LogError(line, `invalid outcome ${outcome}`)
71:       }
72:       jobs.set(id, { id, duration, outcomes: words.slice(3) })
73:     } else if (words[0] === 'submit') {
74:       if (words.length !== 3) throw new LogError(line, 'expected submit <at> <id>')
75:       const at = count(line, 'at', words[1])
76:       const id = words[2]
77:       if (!ID.test(id)) throw new LogError(line, `invalid job id ${id}`)
78:       if (submitted.has(id)) throw new LogError(line, `job ${id} is submitted twice`)
79:       submitted.set(id, line)
80:       submissions.push({ id, at })
81:     } else {
82:       throw new LogError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
83:     }
84:   }
85:   for (const { id } of submissions) {
86:     if (!jobs.has(id)) throw new LogError(0, `unknown job ${id}`)
87:   }
88:   return { jobs, submissions }
89: }

1: /** The simulation: one worker and a rate limit on starts. */
2: 
3: import { createClock } from './clock.js'
4: 
5: /**
6:  * Run every submission to a verdict.
7:  * @param {Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>} jobs - the declared jobs.
8:  * @param {{id: string, at: number}[]} submissions - the submissions, in input order.
9:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}}} policy - the rate limit in force.
10:  * @returns {{attempts: {start: number, id: string, attempt: number, outcome: string, finish: number}[], end: number}} the attempts in the order they started and the clock at the end.
11:  */
12: export function run(jobs, submissions, policy) {
13:   const clock = createClock()
14:   const queued = submissions.map((submission, order) => ({ ...submission, order, readyAt: submission.at, attempt: 0 }))
15:   const attempts = []
16:   const starts = []
17:   while (queued.length > 0) {
18:     let pick = 0
19:     for (const [index, entry] of queued.entries()) {
20:       const best = queued[pick]
21:       if (entry.readyAt < best.readyAt || (entry.readyAt === best.readyAt && entry.order < best.order)) pick = index
22:     }
23:     const entry = queued.splice(pick, 1)[0]
24:     clock.advanceTo(entry.readyAt)
25:     if (policy.limit !== undefined && starts.length >= policy.limit.starts) {
26:       const oldest = starts[starts.length - policy.limit.starts]
27:       if (clock.now() - oldest < policy.limit.window) clock.advanceTo(oldest + policy.limit.window)
28:     }
29:     const job = jobs.get(entry.id)
30:     const start = clock.now()
31:     starts.push(start)
32:     const attempt = entry.attempt + 1
33:     const outcome = job.outcomes[Math.min(attempt, job.outcomes.length) - 1]
34:     const finish = start + job.duration
35:     clock.advanceTo(finish)
36:     attempts.push({ start, id: entry.id, attempt, outcome, finish })
37:   }
38:   return { attempts, end: clock.now() }
39: }

</content>

1: /** The repository's own suite, covering what `jobq` already does. */
2: 
3: import assert from 'node:assert/strict'
4: import { spawnSync } from 'node:child_process'
5: import { test } from 'node:test'
6: import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url'
7: 
8: const cli = fileURLToPath(new URL('../src/cli.js', import.meta.url))
9: const root = fileURLToPath(new URL('../', import.meta.url))
10: 
11: function run(argv, stdin = '') {
12:   const result = spawnSync(process.execPath, [cli, ...argv], { cwd: root, encoding: 'utf8', input: stdin })
13:   return { code: result.status, out: result.stdout, err: result.stderr }
14: }
15: 
16: const TWO = 'job a 5 ok\njob b 3 fail\nsubmit 0 a\nsubmit 0 b\n'
17: 
18: test('one worker runs the submissions in ready order', () => {
19:   assert.deepEqual(run(['trace'], TWO), {
20:     code: 0,
21:     out: '0 a attempt=1 ok finish=5\n5 b attempt=1 fail finish=8\nend 8\n',
22:     err: '',
23:   })
24: })
25: 
26: test('a job submitted later waits for the clock to reach it', () => {
27:   const log = 'job a 1 ok\njob b 1 ok\nsubmit 40 a\nsubmit 0 b\n'
28:   assert.equal(run(['trace'], log).out, '0 b attempt=1 ok finish=1\n40 a attempt=1 ok finish=41\nend 41\n')
29: })
30: 
31: test('two jobs ready at once are taken in submission order', () => {
32:   const log = 'job z 1 ok\njob a 1 ok\nsubmit 0 z\nsubmit 0 a\n'
33:   assert.equal(run(['trace'], log).out, '0 z attempt=1 ok finish=1\n1 a attempt=1 ok finish=2\nend 2\n')
34: })
35: 
36: test('the rate limit holds a start back until the window has room', () => {
37:   const log = 'limit 2 10\njob a 1 ok\njob b 1 ok\njob c 1 ok\nsubmit 0 a\nsubmit 0 b\nsubmit 0 c\n'
38:   assert.equal(
39:     run(['trace'], log).out,
40:     '0 a attempt=1 ok finish=1\n1 b attempt=1 ok finish=2\n10 c attempt=1 ok finish=11\nend 11\n',
41:   )
42: })
43: 
44: test('a job of zero duration finishes in the instant it starts', () => {
45:   assert.equal(run(['trace'], 'job a 0 ok\nsubmit 7 a\n').out, '7 a attempt=1 ok finish=7\nend 7\n')
46: })
47: 
48: test('summary lists the submitted jobs in ascending id order', () => {
49:   assert.deepEqual(run(['summary'], TWO), { code: 0, out: 'a attempts=1 ok\nb attempts=1 fail\nend 8\n', err: '' })
50: })
51: 
52: test('a declared job nothing submits never runs', () => {
53:   assert.equal(run(['summary'], 'job a 1 ok\njob b 1 ok\nsubmit 0 b\n').out, 'b attempts=1 ok\nend 1\n')
54: })
55: 
56: test('an empty log runs nothing and ends at zero', () => {
57:   assert.deepEqual(run(['trace'], ''), { code: 0, out: 'end 0\n', err: '' })
58: })
59: 
60: test('comments and blank lines are ignored', () => {
61:   assert.equal(run(['trace'], '# queue\n\njob a 1 ok\nsubmit 0 a\n').out, '0 a attempt=1 ok finish=1\nend 1\n')
62: })
63: 
64: test('a job line without an outcome is refused', () => {
65:   assert.deepEqual(run(['trace'], 'job a 1\n'), { code: 2, out: '', err: 'error: line 1: expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...\n' })
66: })
67: 
68: test('an outcome word outside ok and fail names its line', () => {
69:   assert.equal(run(['trace'], 'job a 1 maybe\n').err, 'error: line 1: invalid outcome maybe\n')
70: })
71: 
72: test('a duration that is not a number names the field', () => {
73:   assert.equal(run(['trace'], 'job a x ok\n').err, 'error: line 1: duration must be a non-negative integer\n')
74: })
75: 
76: test('a limit of zero starts names the field', () => {
77:   assert.equal(run(['trace'], 'limit 0 10\n').err, 'error: line 1: starts must be a positive integer\n')
78: })
79: 
80: test('a second limit line names its own line', () => {
81:   assert.equal(run(['trace'], 'limit 1 1\nlimit 2 2\n').err, 'error: line 2: limit is declared twice\n')

`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It reads a build graph from standard input and takes one of three argument forms: `waves`, `explain`, or `pack` followed by a worker count. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace.

A `task <name> <cost>` line declares a task. A name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. A cost is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without separators, so `01` is the cost 1. A `dep <name> <dependency>...` line makes the first name depend on every later name on the line; a repeated edge counts once, and a `dep` line may appear before the tasks it names. Every name a `dep` line uses must be declared by some `task` line somewhere in the input. An empty input is a valid graph with no task.

`waves` prints one line per wave, `wave K: ` followed by the wave's task names in ascending order separated by single spaces, and then a final line `total T`. Wave 0 holds every task with no dependency and wave K holds every task whose deepest dependency is in wave K-1. `T` is the makespan with unlimited workers: the greatest finish time, or 0 when there is no task. A task's start is the greatest finish of its dependencies, or 0 when it has none, and its finish is its start plus its cost.

`explain` prints one line per task in ascending name order, `<name> start=<s> finish=<f> depth=<d>`, where the start and finish are the ones above and the depth is the wave the task sits in, and then the same final `total T` line.

`pack <workers>` simulates the same graph on that many workers. Time starts at 0. While a worker is free at the current instant and some task is ready, meaning every one of its dependencies has already finished at or before that instant, take the ready task with the greatest priority, breaking ties by ascending name, and start it on the free worker with the smallest index. A task's priority is the cost of the longest chain that begins at it, counting its own cost and then the costs down to any task that nothing depends on. A task of cost 0 finishes at the instant it starts, so its worker is free again at once and its dependents may start in the same instant. When nothing more can start, time advances to the next instant at which a worker becomes free, and the loop repeats. The output is one line per worker in index order, `worker <i>:` followed by ` <name>@<start>-<finish>` for each task it ran in the order it ran them, and then a final line `makespan M` holding the greatest finish, or 0 when there is no task.

A cycle makes the graph unschedulable: write `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exit 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task.

Every other failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js waves|explain|pack <workers>` when the arguments are not one of the three forms; `error: workers must be a positive integer` when the worker count is not a decimal integer of at least 1 written without a sign or a leading zero; `error: line N: expected task <name> <cost>` and `error: line N: expected dep <name> <dependency>...` when a directive has the wrong number of words; `error: line N: invalid task name <name>` for a name outside the allowed characters; `error: line N: cost must be a non-negative integer`; `error: line N: task <name> is declared twice`; `error: line N: unknown directive <word>`; and `error: unknown task <name>`, with no line number, for the first name in input order that a `dep` line uses and no `task` line declares. goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It reads a build graph from standard input and takes one of three argument forms: `waves`, `explain`, or `pack` followed by a worker count. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace.

A `task <name> <cost>` line declares a task. A name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. A cost is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without separators, so `01` is the cost 1. A `dep <name> <dependency>...` line makes the first name depend on every later name on the line; a repeated edge counts once, and a `dep` line may appear before the tasks it names. Every name a `dep` line uses must be declared by some `task` line somewhere in the input. An empty input is a valid graph with no task.

`waves` prints one line per wave, `wave K: ` followed by the wave's task names in ascending order separated by single spaces, and then a final line `total T`. Wave 0 holds every task with no dependency and wave K holds every task whose deepest dependency is in wave K-1. `T` is the makespan with unlimited workers: the greatest finish time, or 0 when there is no task. A task's start is the greatest finish of its dependencies, or 0 when it has none, and its finish is its start plus its cost.

`explain` prints one line per task in ascending name order, `<name> start=<s> finish=<f> depth=<d>`, where the start and finish are the ones above and the depth is the wave the task sits in, and then the same final `total T` line.

`pack <workers>` simulates the same graph on that many workers. Time starts at 0. While a worker is free at the current instant and some task is ready, meaning every one of its dependencies has already finished at or before that instant, take the ready task with the greatest priority, breaking ties by ascending name, and start it on the free worker with the smallest index. A task's priority is the cost of the longest chain that begins at it, counting its own cost and then the costs down to any task that nothing depends on. A task of cost 0 finishes at the instant it starts, so its worker is free again at once and its dependents may start in the same instant. When nothing more can start, time advances to the next instant at which a worker becomes free, and the loop repeats. The output is one line per worker in index order, `worker <i>:` followed by ` <name>@<start>-<finish>` for each task it ran in the order it ran them, and then a final line `makespan M` holding the greatest finish, or 0 when there is no task.

A cycle makes the graph unschedulable: write `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exit 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task.

Every other failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js waves|explain|pack <workers>` when the arguments are not one of the three forms; `error: workers must be a positive integer` when the worker count is not a decimal integer of at least 1 written without a sign or a leading zero; `error: line N: expected task <name> <cost>` and `error: line N: expected dep <name> <dependency>...` when a directive has the wrong number of words; `error: line N: invalid task name <name>` for a name outside the allowed characters; `error: line N: cost must be a non-negative integer`; `error: line N: task <name> is declared twice`; `error: line N: unknown directive <word>`; and `error: unknown task <name>`, with no line number, for the first name in input order that a `dep` line uses and no `task` line declares. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `tokens` or `stats`, reads UTF-8 source text from standard input, and scans it. Exit 0 when the whole input scans.

Positions count from 1. Reading a line feed moves to the next line and sets the column back to 1. Reading a tab moves the column forward to the next multiple of 4 plus 1, so a tab in column 1 lands on column 5 and a tab in column 6 lands on column 9. Every other code point moves the column forward by 1. A token's position is where its first code point sits.

Spaces, tabs, carriage returns and line feeds separate tokens and produce none. `//` starts a comment that runs to the next line feed or to the end of the input. `/*` starts a block comment that ends at the matching `*/` and nests, so `/* a /* b */ c */` is one comment; a block comment that never closes is an error reported at the `/*` that opened the outermost one.

An identifier starts with a letter or `_` and continues with letters, digits and `_`; it is a `keyword` when it is exactly `let`, `if`, `else`, `while`, `return`, `true`, `false` or `null`, and an `ident` otherwise. A `number` starts with a digit. `0x` or `0X` introduces hexadecimal digits, `0b` or `0B` binary, and `0o` or `0O` octal; anything else is decimal digits, optionally a `.` and more digits, and optionally `e` or `E`, an optional `+` or `-`, and more digits. A `.` only continues a number when a digit follows it, and an exponent marker only continues one when a digit, or a sign and then a digit, follows it. A `_` may sit between two digits of the same run and nowhere else. A number followed immediately by a letter, a digit or `_` that the rules above did not consume, and a prefix with no digit after it, are both errors, and the reported text is everything the scanner ran through, up to and including those trailing characters.

A `string` is written between double quotes and carries the escapes `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\\`, `\"`, `\0`, `\xHH` with exactly two hexadecimal digits, and `\u{H...}` with at least one hexadecimal digit naming a code point of at most 10FFFF. Any other escape is an error reported at its backslash. A line feed inside a string is an error reported where the line feed sits, and a string the input ends before closing is an error reported at its opening quote. A `rawstring` is written `r"` then any characters, line feeds included, up to the first `"`; it carries no escapes, its position is that of the `r`, and an input that ends before the closing `"` is an `unterminated string` reported at that `r` rather than at the quote after it.

The punctuation, matched longest first, is `==`, `!=`, `<=`, `>=`, `&&`, `||`, `->`, `=>`, `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `=`, `<`, `>`, `!`, `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[`, `]`, `,`, `;` and `.`. Any other character is an error.

`tokens` prints one line per token, `<line>:<column> <kind> <body>`. For a `string` and a `rawstring` the body is the decoded value written as a JSON string, quotes and escapes included; for every other kind it is the source text of the token. `stats` instead prints one line per kind, `<kind> <count>`, for all six kinds `ident`, `keyword`, `number`, `punct`, `rawstring` and `string` in that order, whether or not any token had that kind, and then `total N`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The message is `error: usage: cli.js tokens|stats` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: <line>:<column>: <reason>` where the reason is one of `unterminated string`, `newline in string`, `unterminated block comment`, `invalid escape \<character>`, `invalid number <text>` and `unexpected character <character>`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `tokens` or `stats`, reads UTF-8 source text from standard input, and scans it. Exit 0 when the whole input scans.

Positions count from 1. Reading a line feed moves to the next line and sets the column back to 1. Reading a tab moves the column forward to the next multiple of 4 plus 1, so a tab in column 1 lands on column 5 and a tab in column 6 lands on column 9. Every other code point moves the column forward by 1. A token's position is where its first code point sits.

Spaces, tabs, carriage returns and line feeds separate tokens and produce none. `//` starts a comment that runs to the next line feed or to the end of the input. `/*` starts a block comment that ends at the matching `*/` and nests, so `/* a /* b */ c */` is one comment; a block comment that never closes is an error reported at the `/*` that opened the outermost one.

An identifier starts with a letter or `_` and continues with letters, digits and `_`; it is a `keyword` when it is exactly `let`, `if`, `else`, `while`, `return`, `true`, `false` or `null`, and an `ident` otherwise. A `number` starts with a digit. `0x` or `0X` introduces hexadecimal digits, `0b` or `0B` binary, and `0o` or `0O` octal; anything else is decimal digits, optionally a `.` and more digits, and optionally `e` or `E`, an optional `+` or `-`, and more digits. A `.` only continues a number when a digit follows it, and an exponent marker only continues one when a digit, or a sign and then a digit, follows it. A `_` may sit between two digits of the same run and nowhere else. A number followed immediately by a letter, a digit or `_` that the rules above did not consume, and a prefix with no digit after it, are both errors, and the reported text is everything the scanner ran through, up to and including those trailing characters.

A `string` is written between double quotes and carries the escapes `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\\`, `\"`, `\0`, `\xHH` with exactly two hexadecimal digits, and `\u{H...}` with at least one hexadecimal digit naming a code point of at most 10FFFF. Any other escape is an error reported at its backslash. A line feed inside a string is an error reported where the line feed sits, and a string the input ends before closing is an error reported at its opening quote. A `rawstring` is written `r"` then any characters, line feeds included, up to the first `"`; it carries no escapes, its position is that of the `r`, and an input that ends before the closing `"` is an `unterminated string` reported at that `r` rather than at the quote after it.

The punctuation, matched longest first, is `==`, `!=`, `<=`, `>=`, `&&`, `||`, `->`, `=>`, `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `=`, `<`, `>`, `!`, `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[`, `]`, `,`, `;` and `.`. Any other character is an error.

`tokens` prints one line per token, `<line>:<column> <kind> <body>`. For a `string` and a `rawstring` the body is the decoded value written as a JSON string, quotes and escapes included; for every other kind it is the source text of the token. `stats` instead prints one line per kind, `<kind> <count>`, for all six kinds `ident`, `keyword`, `number`, `punct`, `rawstring` and `string` in that order, whether or not any token had that kind, and then `total N`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The message is `error: usage: cli.js tokens|stats` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: <line>:<column>: <reason>` where the reason is one of `unterminated string`, `newline in string`, `unterminated block comment`, `invalid escape \<character>`, `invalid number <text>` and `unexpected character <character>`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `merge`, `merge2` or `regions`, and reads three documents from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; a line that is exactly `%%%` separates the documents, and every other line belongs to the document it sits in. The three documents, in order, are mine, the base they both derive from, and theirs. A document may hold no line at all. Exit 0 when the merge is clean and 1 when any conflict was written, on every mode.

Compare each side against the base with a longest common subsequence over whole lines, comparing them as exact strings. When two subsequences are equally long, take the one whose matches come earliest: walking both documents from the start, take a match whenever the two current lines are equal, and otherwise advance the side whose remaining subsequence is at least as long as the other's, preferring to advance the base when they tie. Every stretch the subsequence does not cover is a change, described as a run of base lines replaced by a run of that side's lines; an insertion replaces zero base lines and a deletion inserts zero lines.

Gather the changes from both sides into one list ordered by where they start in the base, with the changes from mine before the changes from theirs when they start at the same place. Walk that list: take the first remaining change, let the region run from its base start to its base end, and keep absorbing the next change while that change starts at or before the region's current end, extending the end to cover it. The base lines before a region and after the last one form stable regions, which the merge keeps unchanged.

A region only one change touches resolves to that side's lines. For a region several changes touch, each side's replacement runs from the smallest start of its own changes, moved back by however far the region begins before those changes do in the base, to the largest end of its own changes, moved forward by however far the region ends after them. With mine's lines, the base lines of the region, and theirs's lines in hand: if mine and theirs are equal the region resolves to mine; otherwise if mine equals the base it resolves to theirs; otherwise if theirs equals the base it resolves to mine; otherwise the region is a conflict.

`merge` prints the resolved lines in order, and writes a conflict as the line `<<<<<<< mine`, then mine's lines, then `||||||| base`, then the base's lines, then `=======`, then theirs's lines, then `>>>>>>> theirs`. `merge2` writes the same thing without the `||||||| base` line and the base's lines. `regions` instead prints one line per region: `stable N`, `mine N`, `theirs N` or `both N`, where N counts the lines the region resolves to and `both` names a region where the two sides made the same change, or `conflict mine=A base=O theirs=B` with the three line counts.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output. Exit 0 when the merge is clean and 1 when any conflict was written, on every mode.\n\nCompare each side against the base with a longest common subsequence over whole lines, comparing them as exact strings. When two subsequences are equally long, take the one whose matches come earliest: walking both documents from the start, take a match whenever the two current lines are equal, and otherwise advance the side whose remaining subsequence is at least as long as the other's, preferring to advance the base when they tie. Every stretch the subsequence does not cover is a change, described as a run of base lines replaced by a run of that side's lines; an insertion replaces zero base lines and a deletion inserts zero lines.\n\nGather the changes from both sides into one list ordered by where they start in the base, with the changes from mine before the changes from theirs when they start at the same place. Walk that list: take the first remaining change, let the region run from its base start to its base end, and keep absorbing the next change while that change starts at or before the region's current end, extending the end to cover it. The base lines before a region and after the last one form stable regions, which the merge keeps unchanged.\n\nA region only one change touches resolves to that side's lines. content.text:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `merge`, `merge2` or `regions`, and reads three documents from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; a line that is exactly `%%%` separates the documents, and every other line belongs to the document it sits in. The three documents, in order, are mine, the base they both derive from, and theirs. A document may hold no line at all. Exit 0 when the merge is clean and 1 when any conflict was written, on every mode.

Compare each side against the base with a longest common subsequence over whole lines, comparing them as exact strings. When two subsequences are equally long, take the one whose matches come earliest: walking both documents from the start, take a match whenever the two current lines are equal, and otherwise advance the side whose remaining subsequence is at least as long as the other's, preferring to advance the base when they tie. Every stretch the subsequence does not cover is a change, described as a run of base lines replaced by a run of that side's lines; an insertion replaces zero base lines and a deletion inserts zero lines.

Gather the changes from both sides into one list ordered by where they start in the base, with the changes from mine before the changes from theirs when they start at the same place. Walk that list: take the first remaining change, let the region run from its base start to its base end, and keep absorbing the next change while that change starts at or before the region's current end, extending the end to cover it. The base lines before a region and after the last one form stable regions, which the merge keeps unchanged.

A region only one change touches resolves to that side's lines. For a region several changes touch, each side's replacement runs from the smallest start of its own changes, moved back by however far the region begins before those changes do in the base, to the largest end of its own changes, moved forward by however far the region ends after them. With mine's lines, the base lines of the region, and theirs's lines in hand: if mine and theirs are equal the region resolves to mine; otherwise if mine equals the base it resolves to theirs; otherwise if theirs equals the base it resolves to mine; otherwise the region is a conflict.

`merge` prints the resolved lines in order, and writes a conflict as the line `<<<<<<< mine`, then mine's lines, then `||||||| base`, then the base's lines, then `=======`, then theirs's lines, then `>>>>>>> theirs`. `merge2` writes the same thing without the `||||||| base` line and the base's lines. `regions` instead prints one line per region: `stable N`, `mine N`, `theirs N` or `both N`, where N counts the lines the region resolves to and `both` names a region where the two sides made the same change, or `conflict mine=A base=O theirs=B` with the three line counts.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js merge|merge2|regions` when the argument is not exactly one of the three mode words, and `error: expected three parts separated by %%%` when the input does not hold exactly three documents.

`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `merge`, `merge2` or `regions`, and reads three documents from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; a line that is exactly `%%%` separates the documents, and every other line belongs to the document it sits in. The three documents, in order, are mine, the base they both derive from, and theirs. A document may hold no line at all. Exit 0 when the merge is clean and 1 when any conflict was written, on every mode.

Compare each side against the base with a longest common subsequence over whole lines, comparing them as exact strings. When two subsequences are equally long, take the one whose matches come earliest: walking both documents from the start, take a match whenever the two current lines are equal, and otherwise advance the side whose remaining subsequence is at least as long as the other's, preferring to advance the base when they tie. Every stretch the subsequence does not cover is a change, described as a run of base lines replaced by a run of that side's lines; an insertion replaces zero base lines and a deletion inserts zero lines.

Gather the changes from both sides into one list ordered by where they start in the base, with the changes from mine before the changes from theirs when they start at the same place. Walk that list: take the first remaining change, let the region run from its base start to its base end, and keep absorbing the next change while that change starts at or before the region's current end, extending the end to cover it. The base lines before a region and after the last one form stable regions, which the merge keeps unchanged.

A region only one change touches resolves to that side's lines. For a region several changes touch, each side's replacement runs from the smallest start of its own changes, moved back by however far the region begins before those changes do in the base, to the largest end of its own changes, moved forward by however far the region ends after them. With mine's lines, the base lines of the region, and theirs's lines in hand: if mine and theirs are equal the region resolves to mine; otherwise if mine equals the base it resolves to theirs; otherwise if theirs equals the base it resolves to mine; otherwise the region is a conflict.

`merge` prints the resolved lines in order, and writes a conflict as the line `<<<<<<< mine`, then mine's lines, then `||||||| base`, then the base's lines, then `=======`, then theirs's lines, then `>>>>>>> theirs`. `merge2` writes the same thing without the `||||||| base` line and the base's lines. `regions` instead prints one line per region: `stable N`, `mine N`, `theirs N` or `both N`, where N counts the lines the region resolves to and `both` names a region where the two sides made the same change, or `conflict mine=A base=O theirs=B` with the three line counts.

The line `candidates <name>...` declares the field. It must appear exactly once, before any ballot, and must name at least one candidate; a name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_` and `-`, and no name may repeat. The line `ballot <count> <candidate>...` records `count` identical ballots ranking those candidates from most to least preferred. The count is a decimal integer of at least 1 written without a sign and without a leading zero, a ballot names at least one candidate, every name must have been declared, and no ballot may name a candidate twice. A ballot need not rank every candidate.

Count in rounds. Every candidate starts continuing. In each round every ballot counts for the first candidate on it that is still continuing; a ballot whose named candidates are all eliminated is exhausted and counts for nobody. Let the active total be the number of ballots that counted for someone. When the active total is 0 the election ends with no winner. When some candidate's count, doubled, is greater than the active total, that candidate wins and the election ends. Otherwise exactly one candidate is eliminated and another round is counted.

The candidate eliminated is the one with the fewest votes in this round. When several tie for fewest, compare them across the rounds already counted, this one included, from the first round onwards: at the first round where their counts are not all equal, keep only those with the fewest votes in that round and compare the survivors the same way from the first round again. ## Summary

I implemented the ranked-choice voting CLI across three files under `src/`:

- **`src/parse.js`** — parses the election text: splits on newlines (dropping the trailing empty entry), trims/skips blank and `#` lines, validates the `candidates` line (declared once, before ballots, valid names, no duplicates) and `ballot` lines (valid positive-integer count, known candidates, no repeats), and throws a `ParseError` carrying the exact error message and line number (or no line number for "no candidates").
- **`src/count.js`** — runs the instant-runoff count: each round tallies ballots to their first continuing candidate, tracks exhausted ballots, checks for a majority winner or a zero-active-total dead end, and otherwise eliminates the round's lowest scorer, breaking ties by scanning prior rounds (including the current one) from the first round onward, narrowing to the round's fewest-and-earliest-differing survivors, and falling back to reverse code-point order when no round separates them. It records a full history of per-round counts to support this.
- **`src/cli.js`** — validates the single `rounds`/`tally` argument, reads all of stdin synchronously, invokes the parser and counter, and formats output exactly as specified (round lines sorted by descending votes then ascending name, `eliminated` lines, `rounds N` for tally, and the final `winner`/`no winner` line). All failures write a single line to stderr and exit 2 with no stdout, per the specified error catalog.

I verified behavior with the provided test suite (`node --test test/*.test.js`, 16/16 passing) plus manual checks for tie-breaking across multiple rounds, zero-active-total endings, invalid names, repeated ballots, malformed counts, and unknown directives. No dependencies were added and `node_modules` is absent; only files under `src/` were changed.

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `rounds` or `tally`, and reads an election from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace. Exit 0 whenever the election parses.

The line `candidates <name>...` declares the field. It must appear exactly once, before any ballot, and must name at least one candidate; a name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_` and `-`, and no name may repeat. The line `ballot <count> <candidate>...` records `count` identical ballots ranking those candidates from most to least preferred. The count is a decimal integer of at least 1 written without a sign and without a leading zero, a ballot names at least one candidate, every name must have been declared, and no ballot may name a candidate twice. A ballot need not rank every candidate.

Count in rounds. Every candidate starts continuing. In each round every ballot counts for the first candidate on it that is still continuing; a ballot whose named candidates are all eliminated is exhausted and counts for nobody. Let the active total be the number of ballots that counted for someone. When the active total is 0 the election ends with no winner. When some candidate's count, doubled, is greater than the active total, that candidate wins and the election ends. Otherwise exactly one candidate is eliminated and another round is counted.

The candidate eliminated is the one with the fewest votes in this round. When several tie for fewest, compare them across the rounds already counted, this one included, from the first round onwards: at the first round where their counts are not all equal, keep only those with the fewest votes in that round and compare the survivors the same way from the first round again. When no round separates them, eliminate the one whose name sorts last by code point.

`rounds` prints, for each round in order, `round K: ` followed by one `<name>=<votes>` for every continuing candidate, separated by single spaces, and then `exhausted=<n>`. Candidates are listed by descending vote count, and by ascending name where counts tie. A round that eliminated someone is followed by the line `eliminated <name>`. `tally` instead prints one line, `rounds N`, holding how many rounds were counted. Both modes end with `winner <name>`, or `no winner` when no candidate ever reached the majority.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. `bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>` declares a token bucket, with a capacity of at least 1, a refill of at least 0, and a period of at least 1. `window <name> <limit> <span>` declares a sliding window, with a limit of at least 0 and a span of at least 1. Two policies may not share a name. `route <prefix> <policy>...` sends every key that starts with that prefix to those policies, in the order written; every policy must already be declared, and two routes may not share a prefix. `event <tick> <key>` is one arrival at that tick, and ticks never go backwards across the file. Once the first event appears no further `bucket`, `window` or `route` line may follow.

Each policy keeps one independent state per key. A key is limited by the route whose prefix it starts with and which is longest among those that match; a key no route matches is always allowed. When an event arrives, every policy on its route first advances to the event's tick, then every one of them is asked, and only when all of them allow it does each of them record it. A denied event changes no policy's stored allowance.

A token bucket holds `capacity` tokens and starts full when a key first reaches it. Advancing it to a tick adds `refill` tokens for every `per` ticks that passed since it last advanced for that key, without ever passing the capacity, and partial periods accumulate exactly: after `n` ticks the bucket holds `refill` times `n` divided by `per` more tokens than it did, and that fraction is never rounded away. It allows a request when it holds at least one whole token, and recording one spends exactly one.

A sliding window remembers the ticks of the requests it recorded for a key. Advancing it to a tick forgets every remembered tick at or before the tick minus the span, so the window covers the `span` ticks ending at the current one. It allows a request when fewer than `limit` ticks remain remembered, and recording one remembers this tick.
