Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.

`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.

`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. 1: # taskrun
2: 
3: A dependency-aware task runner with no dependencies of its own. It reads a task file from standard input and answers questions about it; it never executes a command.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/parse.js` | the task-file grammar and the refusals it words, as `ParseError` |
11: | `src/graph.js` | run order over the dependency edges |
12: | `src/digest.js` | the FNV-1a digest the snapshot format records |
13: 
14: `test/taskrun.test.js` is the suite for what is already here. `data/files/` holds the workspace files the examples name, and `data/snapshots/` the digest snapshots.
15: 
16: ## The task file
17: 
18: One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace.
19: 
20: ```
21: # build.tasks
22: task build node build.js
23: task bundle node bundle.js
24: needs bundle build
25: ```
26: 
27: `task <name> <word>...` declares a task whose command is the remaining words joined with single spaces. `needs <name> <dependency>...` adds dependencies; a repeated edge counts once, and a `needs` line may stand before the `task` line it names.
28: 
29: ## Modes
30: 
31: - `order` prints the task names one per line, in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose dependencies have all been printed.
32: - `show <name>` prints `<name>: <command>` and then `needs: ` followed by the dependencies in ascending order, or `-` when there are none.
33: - `digest <path>...` prints `<path> <digest>` for each path in argument order, with `missing` in place of a digest for a path that is not there. The digest is 32-bit FNV-1a over the file's bytes — offset basis `0x811c9dc5`, prime `16777619`, xor then multiply — as eight lowercase hex digits.
34: 
35: ## Failures
36: 
37: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A parse failure names its 1-based input line: `error: line 2: unknown directive run`. The messages are `expected task <name> <word>...`, `expected needs <name> <dependency>...`, `invalid task name <name>`, `task <name> is declared twice` and `unknown directive <word>`. A `needs` line naming a task no `task` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown task <name>`, and so is `show` on such a name.
38: 
39: ## Known gaps
40: 
41: `order` does not detect a dependency cycle: it stops as soon as nothing is ready and leaves every task in the cycle out of its output. The task file has no way to declare which files a task reads or writes, so nothing here can tell whether a task is up to date.

(End of file - total 41 lines)
</content>

5: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line it was read from, or 0 when it names none. */
6: export class ParseError extends Error {
7:   /**
8:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names no line.
9:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the `error: ` prefix.
10:    */
11:   constructor(line, message) {
12:     super(message)
13:     this.name = 'ParseError'
14:     this.line = line
15:   }
16: }
17: 
18: /** Whether a word is a usable task name. */
19: function isName(word) {
20:   return NAME.test(word)
21: }
22: 
23: /**
24:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
25:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
26:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
27:  */
28: export function splitLines(text) {
29:   const split = text.split('\n')
30:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
31:   return split
32: }
33: 
34: /**
35:  * Parse a task file into its tasks.
36:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
37:  * @returns {Map<string, {name: string, command: string, needs: string[]}>} the tasks by name, in declaration order.
38:  */
39: export function parse(lines) {
40:   const tasks = new Map()
41:   const referenced = []
42:   const attachments = []
43:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
44:     const line = index + 1
45:     const text = raw.trim()
46:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
47:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
48:     if (words[0] === 'task') {
49:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, 'expected task <name> <word>...')
50:       const name = words[1]
51:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
52:       if (tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `task ${name} is declared twice`)
53:       tasks.set(name, { name, command: words.slice(2).join(' '), needs: [] })
54:     } else if (words[0] === 'needs') {
55:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, 'expected needs <name> <dependency>...')
56:       const [, name, ...values] = words
57:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
58:       referenced.push(name)
59:       for (const value of values) {
60:         if (!isName(value)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${value}`)
61:         referenced.push(value)
62:       }
63:       attachments.push({ name, values })
64:     } else {
65:       throw new ParseError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
66:     }
67:   }
68:   for (const name of referenced) {
69:     if (!tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(0, `unknown task ${name}`)
70:   }
71:   for (const { name, values } of attachments) {
72:     const list = tasks.get(name).needs
73:     for (const value of values) {
74:       if (!list.includes(value)) list.push(value)
75:     }
76:   }
77:   return tasks
78: }

1: /** Ordering the task graph. */
2: 
3: /**
4:  * The tasks in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose
5:  * dependencies have all been emitted. A cycle has no such task, so the order
6:  * stops early and leaves the tasks in it out.
7:  * @param {Map<string, {needs: string[]}>} tasks - the parsed tasks.
8:  * @returns {string[]} the names in run order.
9:  */
10: export function order(tasks) {
11:   const remaining = new Set(tasks.keys())
12:   const emitted = new Set()
13:   const out = []
14:   while (remaining.size > 0) {
15:     const ready = [...remaining].filter(name => tasks.get(name).needs.every(need => emitted.has(need))).sort()
16:     if (ready.length === 0) break
17:     remaining.delete(ready[0])
18:     emitted.add(ready[0])
19:     out.push(ready[0])
20:   }
21:   return out
22: }

3: const OFFSET = 0x811c9dc5

6: /**

8:  * @param {Buffer} bytes - the bytes to digest.
9:  * @returns {string} the digest.
10:  */
11: export function digestBytes(bytes) {
12:   let hash = OFFSET >>> 0
13:   for (const byte of bytes) {
14:     hash = (hash ^ byte) >>> 0
15:     hash = Math.imul(hash, PRIME) >>> 0
16:   }

1: /** The task-file parser: directives to tasks, with the failures the specification words. */
2: 
3: const NAME = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: const PATH = /^[A-Za-z0-9_./-]+$/

6: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line it was read from, or 0 when it names none. */
7: export class ParseError extends Error {
8:   /**
9:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names no line.
10:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the `error: ` prefix.
11:    */
12:   constructor(line, message) {
13:     super(message)
14:     this.name = 'ParseError'
15:     this.line = line
16:   }
17: }
18: 
19: /** Whether a word is a usable task name. */
20: function isName(word) {
21:   return NAME.test(word)
22: }
23: 
24: /** Whether a word is a usable path: the allowed characters, not rooted, no `..` segment. */
25: function isPath(word) {
26:   if (!PATH.test(word)) return false
27:   if (word.startsWith('/')) return false
28:   return !word.split('/').includes('..')
29: }
30: 
31: /**
32:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
33:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
34:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
35:  */
36: export function splitLines(text) {
37:   const split = text.split('\n')
38:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
39:   return split
40: }
41: 
42: /**
43:  * Parse a task file into its tasks.
44:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
45:  * @returns {Map<string, {name: string, command: string, needs: string[]}>} the tasks by name, in declaration order.
46:  */
47: export function parse(lines) {
48:   const tasks = new Map()
49:   const referenced = []
50:   const attachments = []
51:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
52:     const line = index + 1
53:     const text = raw.trim()
54:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
55:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
56:     if (words[0] === 'task') {
57:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, 'expected task <name> <word>...')
58:       const name = words[1]
59:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
60:       if (tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `task ${name} is declared twice`)
61:       tasks.set(name, { name, command: words.slice(2).join(' '), needs: [] })
62:     } else if (words[0] === 'needs') {
63:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, 'expected needs <name> <dependency>...')
64:       const [, name, ...values] = words
65:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
66:       referenced.push(name)
67:       for (const value of values) {
68:         if (!isName(value)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${value}`)
69:         referenced.push(value)
70:       }
71:       attachments.push({ name, values })
72:     } else {
73:       throw new ParseError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
74:     }
75:   }
76:   for (const name of referenced) {
77:     if (!tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(0, `unknown task ${name}`)
78:   }
79:   for (const { name, values } of attachments) {
80:     const list = tasks.get(name).needs
81:     for (const value of values) {
82:       if (!list.includes(value)) list.push(value)
83:     }
84:   }
85:   return tasks

`bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>` declares a token bucket, with a capacity of at least 1, a refill of at least 0, and a period of at least 1. `window <name> <limit> <span>` declares a sliding window, with a limit of at least 0 and a span of at least 1. Two policies may not share a name. `route <prefix> <policy>...` sends every key that starts with that prefix to those policies, in the order written; every policy must already be declared, and two routes may not share a prefix. `event <tick> <key>` is one arrival at that tick, and ticks never go backwards across the file. Once the first event appears no further `bucket`, `window` or `route` line may follow.

Each policy keeps one independent state per key. A key is limited by the route whose prefix it starts with and which is longest among those that match; a key no route matches is always allowed. When an event arrives, every policy on its route first advances to the event's tick, then every one of them is asked, and only when all of them allow it does each of them record it. A denied event changes no policy's stored allowance.

A token bucket holds `capacity` tokens and starts full when a key first reaches it. Advancing it to a tick adds `refill` tokens for every `per` ticks that passed since it last advanced for that key, without ever passing the capacity, and partial periods accumulate exactly: after `n` ticks the bucket holds `refill` times `n` divided by `per` more tokens than it did, and that fraction is never rounded away. It allows a request when it holds at least one whole token, and recording one spends exactly one.

A sliding window remembers the ticks of the requests it recorded for a key. Advancing it to a tick forgets every remembered tick at or before the tick minus the span, so the window covers the `span` ticks ending at the current one. It allows a request when fewer than `limit` ticks remain remembered, and recording one remembers this tick.

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `replay` or `summary`, and reads a limiter file from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace. Exit 0 whenever the file parses.

A name, a route prefix and an event key are each one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/`, `:` and `-`. Every count is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without a leading zero unless it is exactly `0`.

`bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>` declares a token bucket, with a capacity of at least 1, a refill of at least 0, and a period of at least 1. `window <name> <limit> <span>` declares a sliding window, with a limit of at least 0 and a span of at least 1. Two policies may not share a name. `route <prefix> <policy>...` sends every key that starts with that prefix to those policies, in the order written; every policy must already be declared, and two routes may not share a prefix. `event <tick> <key>` is one arrival at that tick, and ticks never go backwards across the file. Once the first event appears no further `bucket`, `window` or `route` line may follow.

Each policy keeps one independent state per key. A key is limited by the route whose prefix it starts with and which is longest among those that match; a key no route matches is always allowed. When an event arrives, every policy on its route first advances to the event's tick, then every one of them is asked, and only when all of them allow it does each of them record it. A denied event changes no policy's stored allowance.

A token bucket holds `capacity` tokens and starts full when a key first reaches it. Advancing it to a tick adds `refill` tokens for every `per` ticks that passed since it last advanced for that key, without ever passing the capacity, and partial periods accumulate exactly: after `n` ticks the bucket holds `refill` times `n` divided by `per` more tokens than it did, and that fraction is never rounded away. It allows a request when it holds at least one whole token, and recording one spends exactly one.

A sliding window remembers the ticks of the requests it recorded for a key. Advancing it to a tick forgets every remembered tick at or before the tick minus the span, so the window covers the `span` ticks ending at the current one. It allows a request when fewer than `limit` ticks remain remembered, and recording one remembers this tick.

`replay` prints one line per event in log order: `<tick> <key> allow`, or `<tick> <key> deny <policy>` naming the first policy on the route, in the order the route wrote them, that refused. `summary` instead prints `<key> allowed=<a> denied=<d>` for every key that saw an event, in ascending key order, and then `total allowed=<a> denied=<d>`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js replay|summary` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: line N: <reason>` where the reason is one of `unknown directive <word>`, `expected bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>`, `expected window <name> <limit> <span>`, `expected route <prefix> <policy>...`, `expected event <tick> <key>`, `invalid policy name <name>`, `invalid route prefix <prefix>`, `invalid key <key>`, `policy <name> is declared twice`, `prefix <prefix> is routed twice`, `unknown policy <name>`, `declarations must come before the first event`, `tick T is before tick P`, and `<field> must be an integer of at least <least>` naming the field as `capacity`, `refill`, `per`, `limit`, `span` or `tick`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

content.text:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `tokens` or `stats`, reads UTF-8 source text from standard input, and scans it. Exit 0 when the whole input scans.

Positions count from 1. Reading a line feed moves to the next line and sets the column back to 1. Reading a tab moves the column forward to the next multiple of 4 plus 1, so a tab in column 1 lands on column 5 and a tab in column 6 lands on column 9. Every other code point moves the column forward by 1. A token's position is where its first code point sits.

Spaces, tabs, carriage returns and line feeds separate tokens and produce none. `//` starts a comment that runs to the next line feed or to the end of the input. `/*` starts a block comment that ends at the matching `*/` and nests, so `/* a /* b */ c */` is one comment; a block comment that never closes is an error reported at the `/*` that opened the outermost one.

An identifier starts with a letter or `_` and continues with letters, digits and `_`; it is a `keyword` when it is exactly `let`, `if`, `else`, `while`, `return`, `true`, `false` or `null`, and an `ident` otherwise. A `number` starts with a digit. `0x` or `0X` introduces hexadecimal digits, `0b` or `0B` binary, and `0o` or `0O` octal; anything else is decimal digits, optionally a `.` and more digits, and optionally `e` or `E`, an optional `+` or `-`, and more digits. A `.` only continues a number when a digit follows it, and an exponent marker only continues one when a digit, or a sign and then a digit, follows it. A `_` may sit between two digits of the same run and nowhere else. A number followed immediately by a letter, a digit or `_` that the rules above did not consume, and a prefix with no digit after it, are both errors, and the reported text is everything the scanner ran through, up to and including those trailing characters.

A `string` is written between double quotes and carries the escapes `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\\`, `\"`, `\0`, `\xHH` with exactly two hexadecimal digits, and `\u{H...}` with at least one hexadecimal digit naming a code point of at most 10FFFF. Any other escape is an error reported at its backslash. A line feed inside a string is an error reported where the line feed sits, and a string the input ends before closing is an error reported at its opening quote. A `rawstring` is written `r"` then any characters, line feeds included, up to the first `"`; it carries no escapes, its position is that of the `r`, and an input that ends before the closing `"` is an `unterminated string` reported at that `r` rather than at the quote after it.

The punctuation, matched longest first, is `==`, `!=`, `<=`, `>=`, `&&`, `||`, `->`, `=>`, `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `=`, `<`, `>`, `!`, `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[`, `]`, `,`, `;` and `.`. Any other character is an error.

`tokens` prints one line per token, `<line>:<column> <kind> <body>`. For a `string` and a `rawstring` the body is the decoded value written as a JSON string, quotes and escapes included; for every other kind it is the source text of the token. `stats` instead prints one line per kind, `<kind> <count>`, for all six kinds `ident`, `keyword`, `number`, `punct`, `rawstring` and `string` in that order, whether or not any token had that kind, and then `total N`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The message is `error: usage: cli.js tokens|stats` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: <line>:<column>: <reason>` where the reason is one of `unterminated string`, `newline in string`, `unterminated block comment`, `invalid escape \<character>`, `invalid number <text>` and `unexpected character <character>`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `tokens` or `stats`, reads UTF-8 source text from standard input, and scans it. Exit 0 when the whole input scans.

Positions count from 1. Reading a line feed moves to the next line and sets the column back to 1. Reading a tab moves the column forward to the next multiple of 4 plus 1, so a tab in column 1 lands on column 5 and a tab in column 6 lands on column 9. Every other code point moves the column forward by 1. A token's position is where its first code point sits.

Spaces, tabs, carriage returns and line feeds separate tokens and produce none. `//` starts a comment that runs to the next line feed or to the end of the input. `/*` starts a block comment that ends at the matching `*/` and nests, so `/* a /* b */ c */` is one comment; a block comment that never closes is an error reported at the `/*` that opened the outermost one.

An identifier starts with a letter or `_` and continues with letters, digits and `_`; it is a `keyword` when it is exactly `let`, `if`, `else`, `while`, `return`, `true`, `false` or `null`, and an `ident` otherwise. A `number` starts with a digit. `0x` or `0X` introduces hexadecimal digits, `0b` or `0B` binary, and `0o` or `0O` octal; anything else is decimal digits, optionally a `.` and more digits, and optionally `e` or `E`, an optional `+` or `-`, and more digits. A `.` only continues a number when a digit follows it, and an exponent marker only continues one when a digit, or a sign and then a digit, follows it. A `_` may sit between two digits of the same run and nowhere else. A number followed immediately by a letter, a digit or `_` that the rules above did not consume, and a prefix with no digit after it, are both errors, and the reported text is everything the scanner ran through, up to and including those trailing characters.

A `string` is written between double quotes and carries the escapes `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\\`, `\"`, `\0`, `\xHH` with exactly two hexadecimal digits, and `\u{H...}` with at least one hexadecimal digit naming a code point of at most 10FFFF. Any other escape is an error reported at its backslash. A line feed inside a string is an error reported where the line feed sits, and a string the input ends before closing is an error reported at its opening quote. A `rawstring` is written `r"` then any characters, line feeds included, up to the first `"`; it carries no escapes, its position is that of the `r`, and an input that ends before the closing `"` is an `unterminated string` reported at that `r` rather than at the quote after it.

The punctuation, matched longest first, is `==`, `!=`, `<=`, `>=`, `&&`, `||`, `->`, `=>`, `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `=`, `<`, `>`, `!`, `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[`, `]`, `,`, `;` and `.`. Any other character is an error.

`tokens` prints one line per token, `<line>:<column> <kind> <body>`. For a `string` and a `rawstring` the body is the decoded value written as a JSON string, quotes and escapes included; for every other kind it is the source text of the token. `stats` instead prints one line per kind, `<kind> <count>`, for all six kinds `ident`, `keyword`, `number`, `punct`, `rawstring` and `string` in that order, whether or not any token had that kind, and then `total N`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The message is `error: usage: cli.js tokens|stats` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: <line>:<column>: <reason>` where the reason is one of `unterminated string`, `newline in string`, `unterminated block comment`, `invalid escape \<character>`, `invalid number <text>` and `unexpected character <character>`. `conflayers` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/conflayers.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the two layered modes its `merge` primitive was built for, make the declared types real, and report a bad value where it was written. Everything `README.md` documents about `dump`, `get`, the INI grammar and the existing failures stays exactly as it is, including every message and every column; the work spans the parser, the schema, the layer stack, and the command.

`load <base> <site>` and `origin <base> <site>` each stack three layers, weakest first: the INI file named by the first argument, the INI file named by the second, and an environment layer read from standard input. A later layer overrides a key an earlier one set, one key at a time, so a file that sets only `server.port` leaves every other key to the layer below it. The layers are read in that order, and a layer's failures are all reported before the next layer is read.

The environment layer is a line per variable. A line is trimmed first; an empty one, and one beginning with `#`, is ignored. The rest is `NAME=VALUE`: the text before the first `=` is the name, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A setting travels under `CONF_` followed by its key uppercased with every `.` replaced by `_`, so `server.port` arrives as `CONF_SERVER_PORT`. Its failures carry a position too, worded `error: <stdin>:<line>:<column>: ` followed by `expected NAME=VALUE` or `expected a variable name` or `unknown environment variable <NAME>` or `<NAME> is set twice`, each reported at the line's first non-space character and each counting columns the way the INI parser does.

Both modes are strict about keys where `dump` is lenient: a key an INI layer sets and the schema does not know fails with `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: unknown setting <key>` at the value's position, and a layer's keys are checked in the order the file writes them, after that file parses. The value's position is the column of its first character, or, when the value is empty, one past the line's last non-space character.

`origin <base> <site>` prints `<key> <layer>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the layer is `base`, `site`, `env`, or `default` when no layer set the key.

`load <base> <site>` prints `<key>=<value>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the value is the winning layer's text coerced by the key's declared type, or the schema default coerced the same way. A `string` is its text. An `integer` is an optional `-` and then digits without a leading zero, unless the number is exactly `0`, and renders as written. A `boolean` is `true` or `false`, lowercase, and renders as written. An `enum` is one of its declared members and renders as written. A `duration` is digits followed by `ms`, `s`, `m` or `h`, and renders as its whole number of milliseconds. A `list` is items separated by commas, each trimmed, with a repeat dropped and the order kept, rendered joined by single commas; empty text is the empty list and renders empty, but an empty item between two commas is a failure. A value that does not fit its type fails with `error: <where>: <message>`, where `<where>` is the file and position it was written at, or `<stdin>` and its position when the environment layer set it, and the message is `<key> is not an integer: <text>`, `<key> is not a boolean: <text>`, `<key> is not one of <members joined by |>: <text>`, `<key> is not a duration: <text>` or `<key> has an empty item: <text>`. The keys are coerced in ascending order, so the first failing key in that order decides.

The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js dump <file>|get <file> <key>|load <base> <site>|origin <base> <site>`; `dump` takes one path, `get` a path and a key, and `load` and `origin` exactly two paths. 1: # conflayers
2: 
3: A configuration loader with no dependencies. It reads INI files, knows a fixed schema of settings, and answers what one of them is set to.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/ini.js` | the INI grammar and the refusals it words, as `IniError`, each with a line and a column |
11: | `src/schema.js` | `SETTINGS`, the known settings with their declared type and default text |
12: | `src/layer.js` | `merge`, which stacks layers so that the last one to set a key wins |
13: 
14: `test/conflayers.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the INI files the examples name.
15: 
16: ## The INI grammar
17: 
18: A line is trimmed first. An empty one, and one beginning with `#` or `;`, is ignored. `[name]` opens a section, and a section may be opened more than once. Anything else is `key = value`: the text before the first `=` is the key, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A key outside a section keeps its own name; a key inside one is prefixed with the section name and a dot, so `port` under `[server]` is `server.port`. A name and a key are one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. Nothing inside a value is special: `#` and `;` open a comment only at the start of a line.
19: 
20: ```ini
21: log.file = /var/log/app.log
22: 
23: [server]
24: port = 9090
25: ```
26: 
27: ## The schema
28: 
29: | Key | Type | Default |
30: | --- | --- | --- |
31: | `log.file` | string | (empty) |
32: | `log.level` | enum `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` | `info` |
33: | `log.rotate` | boolean | `true` |
34: | `retry.attempts` | integer | `3` |
35: | `retry.backoff` | duration | `250ms` |
36: | `server.host` | string | `localhost` |
37: | `server.port` | integer | `8080` |
38: | `server.timeout` | duration | `30s` |
39: | `server.tls` | boolean | `false` |
40: | `tags` | list | (empty) |
41: 
42: The types are declared but nothing here enforces them yet: every mode below prints the raw text as the file wrote it.
43: 
44: ## Modes
45: 
46: - `dump <file>` prints `<key>=<raw text>` for every schema key in ascending order, falling back to the schema default for a key the file leaves out. A key the schema does not know is ignored.
47: - `get <file> <key>` prints the raw text of one setting, or its default. A key outside the schema is refused.
48: 
49: ## Failures
50: 
51: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure carries the position it was read at, as `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: <message>`, where the column counts characters of the raw line from 1, leading whitespace included. The messages are `expected "]"`, reported one past the line's last non-space character; `expected a section name` and `invalid section name <name>`, at the name's first character; `expected a section header or key = value` and `invalid key <key>`, at the line's first non-space character; `expected a key`, at the `=`; and `key <key> is set twice`, at the line's first non-space character. A file that cannot be read is refused as `error: cannot read <path>`, an unknown key as `error: unknown setting <key>`, and a malformed argument list with the usage line.
52: 
53: ## Known gaps
54: 
55: Only one file is ever read, so the `merge` primitive stacks a single layer and nothing overrides anything. Nothing reads the environment. The declared types do nothing: `server.port = eighty` loads as happily as `server.port = 80`, and a caller has to coerce the text itself. `IniError` carries a position, but the parse result does not, so nothing downstream could say where a bad value was written.

1: /** The INI reader: dotted keys and the raw text of each value. */
2: 
3: const NAME = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: 
5: /** One refusal of an INI line, carrying the 1-based line and column it was read at. */
6: export class IniError extends Error {
7:   /**
8:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line.
9:    * @param {number} column - the 1-based column of the raw line.
10:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
11:    */
12:   constructor(line, column, message) {
13:     super(message)
14:     this.name = 'IniError'
15:     this.line = line
16:     this.column = column
17:   }
18: }
19: 
20: /** The 1-based column of the first non-space character of `raw`. */
21: function indent(raw) {
22:   return raw.length - raw.trimStart().length + 1
23: }
24: 
25: /**
26:  * Parse INI text into its settings.
27:  * @param {string} text - the file's whole text.
28:  * @returns {Map<string, string>} each dotted key's raw value, in the order the file writes them.
29:  * @throws {IniError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
30:  */
31: export function parse(text) {
32:   const lines = text.split('\n')
33:   if (lines.length > 0 && lines[lines.length - 1] === '') lines.pop()
34:   const values = new Map()
35:   let section = ''
36:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
37:     const line = index + 1
38:     const trimmed = raw.trim()
39:     if (trimmed === '' || trimmed.startsWith('#') || trimmed.startsWith(';')) continue
40:     if (trimmed.startsWith('[')) {
41:       if (!trimmed.endsWith(']')) throw new IniError(line, raw.trimEnd().length + 1, 'expected "]"')
42:       const name = trimmed.slice(1, -1)
43:       if (name === '') throw new IniError(line, indent(raw) + 1, 'expected a section name')
44:       if (!NAME.test(name)) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw) + 1, `invalid section name ${name}`)
45:       section = name
46:       continue
47:     }
48:     const split = trimmed.indexOf('=')
49:     if (split === -1) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw), 'expected a section header or key = value')
50:     const key = trimmed.slice(0, split).trim()
51:     if (key === '') throw new IniError(line, indent(raw) + split, 'expected a key')
52:     if (!NAME.test(key)) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw), `invalid key ${key}`)
53:     const full = section === '' ? key : `${section}.${key}`
54:     if (values.has(full)) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw), `key ${full} is set twice`)
55:     values.set(full, trimmed.slice(split + 1).trim())
56:   }
57:   return values
58: }

goal.objective:
`conflayers` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/conflayers.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the two layered modes its `merge` primitive was built for, make the declared types real, and report a bad value where it was written. Everything `README.md` documents about `dump`, `get`, the INI grammar and the existing failures stays exactly as it is, including every message and every column; the work spans the parser, the schema, the layer stack, and the command.

`load <base> <site>` and `origin <base> <site>` each stack three layers, weakest first: the INI file named by the first argument, the INI file named by the second, and an environment layer read from standard input. A later layer overrides a key an earlier one set, one key at a time, so a file that sets only `server.port` leaves every other key to the layer below it. The layers are read in that order, and a layer's failures are all reported before the next layer is read.

The environment layer is a line per variable. A line is trimmed first; an empty one, and one beginning with `#`, is ignored. The rest is `NAME=VALUE`: the text before the first `=` is the name, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A setting travels under `CONF_` followed by its key uppercased with every `.` replaced by `_`, so `server.port` arrives as `CONF_SERVER_PORT`. Its failures carry a position too, worded `error: <stdin>:<line>:<column>: ` followed by `expected NAME=VALUE` or `expected a variable name` or `unknown environment variable <NAME>` or `<NAME> is set twice`, each reported at the line's first non-space character and each counting columns the way the INI parser does.

Both modes are strict about keys where `dump` is lenient: a key an INI layer sets and the schema does not know fails with `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: unknown setting <key>` at the value's position, and a layer's keys are checked in the order the file writes them, after that file parses. The value's position is the column of its first character, or, when the value is empty, one past the line's last non-space character.

`origin <base> <site>` prints `<key> <layer>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the layer is `base`, `site`, `env`, or `default` when no layer set the key.

`load <base> <site>` prints `<key>=<value>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the value is the winning layer's text coerced by the key's declared type, or the schema default coerced the same way. A `string` is its text. An `integer` is an optional `-` and then digits without a leading zero, unless the number is exactly `0`, and renders as written. A `boolean` is `true` or `false`, lowercase, and renders as written. An `enum` is one of its declared members and renders as written. A `duration` is digits followed by `ms`, `s`, `m` or `h`, and renders as its whole number of milliseconds. A `list` is items separated by commas, each trimmed, with a repeat dropped and the order kept, rendered joined by single commas; empty text is the empty list and renders empty, but an empty item between two commas is a failure. A value that does not fit its type fails with `error: <where>: <message>`, where `<where>` is the file and position it was written at, or `<stdin>` and its position when the environment layer set it, and the message is `<key> is not an integer: <text>`, `<key> is not a boolean: <text>`, `<key> is not one of <members joined by |>: <text>`, `<key> is not a duration: <text>` or `<key> has an empty item: <text>`. The keys are coerced in ascending order, so the first failing key in that order decides.

The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js dump <file>|get <file> <key>|load <base> <site>|origin <base> <site>`; `dump` takes one path, `get` a path and a key, and `load` and `origin` exactly two paths. `src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `json` or `keys`, and reads a configuration document from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every directive fits on one line. Exit 0 whenever the document parses.

A line whose first character that is not a space or a tab is `#` or `;`, and a line holding only spaces and tabs, contributes nothing. Elsewhere a `#` or a `;` outside a quoted string ends the line, and what follows it is ignored; a `#` that a value runs into without whitespace before it is part of that value's text and makes it invalid.

A name is a bare word of one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_` and `-`, or a quoted string. A dotted name is names joined by `.`, with spaces and tabs allowed around each `.`.

A line beginning with `[` is a header. `[name]` makes that table current, creating the tables on the way; when the name already holds anything other than a table the reason is `<path> is not a table`, and otherwise a table a header already made current may not be named by a second `[name]` header, though a table that only came into being on the way to a deeper one, or from a dotted key, still may. `[[name]]` appends a fresh table to the array of tables at that name, creating it when it is absent, and makes that fresh table current; when the name already holds anything other than an array of tables the reason is `<path> is not an array of tables`. Walking through an array of tables uses its last element. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the closing bracket is an error.

Every other line is `<dotted name> = <value>`, assigning inside the current table, creating the tables the dots walk through. A name already holding anything may not be assigned again, and a dot may not walk through a name that holds something other than a table or an array of tables.

A value is one of: `true` or `false`; an integer, an optional `+` or `-` and runs of digits joined by single `_`; a float, an integer with a fraction of `.` and digit runs, an exponent of `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digit runs, or both; a basic string in double quotes carrying the escapes `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\0` and `\uXXXX` with exactly four hexadecimal digits; a literal string in single quotes carrying no escapes; an array of values in `[` and `]`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing one trailing comma; or an inline table of `<dotted name> = <value>` pairs in `{` and `}`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing no trailing comma. Arrays and inline tables may hold each other. A bare word that is none of these is an error naming that word, while a value required but never written, because the line ends or a `,`, a `]` or a `}` comes first, is `expected a value`. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the value is an error.

`json` prints the document as JSON indented by two spaces, with the members of every object in ascending key order by code point, and a trailing newline; an array of tables prints as a JSON array, and a float prints however JSON prints its number, so a float that happens to be whole prints without a fraction. `keys` instead prints one line per node below the root, `<path> <type>`, walking objects in ascending key order and arrays in index order, depth first, each node before its children. A path joins object keys with `.` and appends `[i]` for an array index, using the key text as written after decoding. The type is `table`, `array`, `string`, `integer`, `float` or `boolean`, and an array of tables is an `array`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The message is `error: usage: cli.js json|keys` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: line N: <reason>` where the reason is one of `expected a name`, `expected a value`, `expected key = value`, `expected = in an inline table`, `unterminated string`, `unterminated array`, `unterminated inline table`, `unterminated table header`, `invalid escape \<character>`, `invalid value <text>`, `trailing text after a value`, `trailing text after a table header`, `key <path> is defined twice` with the path counted from the root, `table <path> is defined twice`, `<path> is not a table`, and `<path> is not an array of tables`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `json` or `keys`, and reads a configuration document from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every directive fits on one line. Exit 0 whenever the document parses.

A line whose first character that is not a space or a tab is `#` or `;`, and a line holding only spaces and tabs, contributes nothing. Elsewhere a `#` or a `;` outside a quoted string ends the line, and what follows it is ignored; a `#` that a value runs into without whitespace before it is part of that value's text and makes it invalid.

A name is a bare word of one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_` and `-`, or a quoted string. A dotted name is names joined by `.`, with spaces and tabs allowed around each `.`.

A line beginning with `[` is a header. `[name]` makes that table current, creating the tables on the way; when the name already holds anything other than a table the reason is `<path> is not a table`, and otherwise a table a header already made current may not be named by a second `[name]` header, though a table that only came into being on the way to a deeper one, or from a dotted key, still may. `[[name]]` appends a fresh table to the array of tables at that name, creating it when it is absent, and makes that fresh table current; when the name already holds anything other than an array of tables the reason is `<path> is not an array of tables`. Walking through an array of tables uses its last element. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the closing bracket is an error.

Every other line is `<dotted name> = <value>`, assigning inside the current table, creating the tables the dots walk through. A name already holding anything may not be assigned again, and a dot may not walk through a name that holds something other than a table or an array of tables.

All 16 tests pass, no `node_modules` present, and manual verification against RFC 3986 §5.4.1/§5.4.2 examples (both normal and abnormal cases) matches exactly. I've implemented:

**`src/uri.js`** — parsing (scheme/authority/userinfo/host/port/path/query/fragment with presence tracking), percent-encoding normalization (uppercase hex, decode unreserved bytes, checked in path→userinfo→host→query→fragment order), ASCII-only lowercasing, default-port dropping, RFC 3986 §5.2.4 dot-segment removal, the empty-path-with-authority→`/` rule, and RFC 3986 §5.2.2/§5.2.3 strict resolution/merging.

**`src/cli.js`** — reads stdin, splits on `\n` dropping the trailing empty tail, buffers all output so a mid-stream failure writes nothing to stdout, and reports the required error messages with correct line numbers, exiting 2 on failure and 0 on success.

Key spec details verified by hand-testing beyond the visible suite:
- Absent vs. empty query/fragment round-trip correctly (`http://a/b?` vs `http://a/b`)
- IPv6 authority `[::1]:80` parses/normalizes correctly (bracket-aware port split)
- Multiple `@` in authority → userinfo is everything before the *last* `@`
- Padded port `:080` is *not* treated as the default and is kept
- Percent-decoding of `%2F` stays encoded (not unreserved) while `%7E`→`~`
- Strict resolution: `http:g` against `http://a/b/c/d;p?q` stays `http:g` (doesn't inherit base authority/path)
- Error precedence: truncated `%` in host reports as `path` when a path-component error also exists, confirming the mandated check order

I walked through the specification sentence by sentence and verified each requirement with a minimal, targeted probe compared byte-for-byte against what the sentence demands:

- **`resolve` splitting on first space**: verified a reference containing spaces round-trips correctly, splitting only on the first space.
- **Scheme parsing boundary**: confirmed a `:` preceded by `/`, `?`, or `#` does *not* count as a scheme delimiter (`a/b:c`, `a?b:c`, `a#b:c` all left scheme-less).

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `normalize` or `resolve`, reads UTF-8 text from standard input, and writes one result line per input line to standard output. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every remaining line is a record, including an empty one. Exit 0 when every record succeeds.

In `normalize` mode each record is one URI reference and its output line is the normalized form. In `resolve` mode each record is a base URI, one space, and a reference; the output line is the reference resolved against the base and then normalized. The first space separates the two, so a reference may contain spaces and a base may not.

Parse a URI reference into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by RFC 3986's generic syntax: an optional scheme running to the first `:`, which may not be preceded by any `/`, `?` or `#`; an optional authority introduced by `//` and running to the next `/`, `?` or `#`; the path up to the next `?` or `#`; an optional query from `?` to the next `#`; an optional fragment from `#` to the end. An absent component and an empty one are different, so `http://a/b?` has an empty query, `http://a/b` has none, and both print back the way they came. Inside an authority the userinfo is everything before the last `@`, the port is everything after the first `:` that follows the last `]`, and the host is what lies between.

Normalization applies in this order. Lowercase the scheme, using ASCII rules only. Normalize percent-encodings in every component: uppercase the two hexadecimal digits of each `%XX`, then replace the triplet with the character it encodes when that character is unreserved, meaning one of `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `-`, `.`, `_` and `~`. Lowercase the host, using ASCII rules only and leaving the userinfo alone. Drop the port when it is written empty or written with exactly the digits of the scheme's default, which is 80 for `http` and `ws`, 443 for `https` and `wss`, and 21 for `ftp`; no other scheme has one, and a port padded with a leading zero is not written with those digits and stays. Remove dot segments from the path by RFC 3986 section 5.2.4, so a `.` segment disappears, a `..` segment removes the segment before it, and a `..` that would climb above the root is discarded. Finally, when an authority is present and the path is empty, make the path `/`. Dot removal never touches the query or the fragment.

Resolve by RFC 3986 section 5.2.2 in its strict form, in which a reference that repeats the base's scheme is still an absolute URI. A reference that writes a scheme is itself the target, with the dot segments removed from its path. A reference that writes an authority takes the base's scheme and keeps everything else of its own. A reference with neither and an empty path takes the base's authority and path, takes the base's query only when it writes no query of its own, and takes its own fragment, which may be absent. Otherwise, when the reference's path does not start with `/`, merge it onto the base's: keep everything of the base path up to and including its last `/`, or use the reference path alone when the base path holds no `/`, except that a base that has an authority and an empty path contributes a single leading `/`. Remove the dot segments from the resulting path, take the base's authority and the reference's query and fragment, and normalize the whole.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js normalize|resolve` when the arguments are not exactly one of the two mode words; `error: line N: expected a base and a reference` when a `resolve` record holds no space; `error: line N: the base has no scheme` when the base of a `resolve` record writes no scheme; and `error: line N: the path has a truncated percent-encoding` when a `%` is not followed by two hexadecimal digits, with `path` replaced by `userinfo`, `host`, `query` or `fragment` for whichever component carries it, those five being checked in that order. N counts records from 1. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `rounds` or `tally`, and reads an election from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace. Exit 0 whenever the election parses.

The line `candidates <name>...` declares the field. It must appear exactly once, before any ballot, and must name at least one candidate; a name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_` and `-`, and no name may repeat. The line `ballot <count> <candidate>...` records `count` identical ballots ranking those candidates from most to least preferred. The count is a decimal integer of at least 1 written without a sign and without a leading zero, a ballot names at least one candidate, every name must have been declared, and no ballot may name a candidate twice. A ballot need not rank every candidate.

Count in rounds. Every candidate starts continuing. In each round every ballot counts for the first candidate on it that is still continuing; a ballot whose named candidates are all eliminated is exhausted and counts for nobody. Let the active total be the number of ballots that counted for someone. When the active total is 0 the election ends with no winner. When some candidate's count, doubled, is greater than the active total, that candidate wins and the election ends. Otherwise exactly one candidate is eliminated and another round is counted.

The candidate eliminated is the one with the fewest votes in this round. When several tie for fewest, compare them across the rounds already counted, this one included, from the first round onwards: at the first round where their counts are not all equal, keep only those with the fewest votes in that round and compare the survivors the same way from the first round again. When no round separates them, eliminate the one whose name sorts last by code point.

`rounds` prints, for each round in order, `round K: ` followed by one `<name>=<votes>` for every continuing candidate, separated by single spaces, and then `exhausted=<n>`. Candidates are listed by descending vote count, and by ascending name where counts tie. A round that eliminated someone is followed by the line `eliminated <name>`. `tally` instead prints one line, `rounds N`, holding how many rounds were counted. Both modes end with `winner <name>`, or `no winner` when no candidate ever reached the majority.

A name, a route prefix and an event key are each one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/`, `:` and `-`. Every count is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without a leading zero unless it is exactly `0`.

`bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>` declares a token bucket, with a capacity of at least 1, a refill of at least 0, and a period of at least 1. `window <name> <limit> <span>` declares a sliding window, with a limit of at least 0 and a span of at least 1. Two policies may not share a name. `route <prefix> <policy>...` sends every key that starts with that prefix to those policies, in the order written; every policy must already be declared, and two routes may not share a prefix. `event <tick> <key>` is one arrival at that tick, and ticks never go backwards across the file. Once the first event appears no further `bucket`, `window` or `route` line may follow.

Each policy keeps one independent state per key. A key is limited by the route whose prefix it starts with and which is longest among those that match; a key no route matches is always allowed. When an event arrives, every policy on its route first advances to the event's tick, then every one of them is asked, and only when all of them allow it does each of them record it. A denied event changes no policy's stored allowance.

A token bucket holds `capacity` tokens and starts full when a key first reaches it. Advancing it to a tick adds `refill` tokens for every `per` ticks that passed since it last advanced for that key, without ever passing the capacity, and partial periods accumulate exactly: after `n` ticks the bucket holds `refill` times `n` divided by `per` more tokens than it did, and that fraction is never rounded away. It allows a request when it holds at least one whole token, and recording one spends exactly one.

A sliding window remembers the ticks of the requests it recorded for a key. Advancing it to a tick forgets every remembered tick at or before the tick minus the span, so the window covers the `span` ticks ending at the current one. It allows a request when fewer than `limit` ticks remain remembered, and recording one remembers this tick.

`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `replay` or `summary`, and reads a limiter file from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace. A name, a route prefix and an event key are each one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/`, `:` and `-`. Every count is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without a leading zero unless it is exactly `0`.

`bucket <name> <capacity> <refill> <per>` declares a token bucket, with a capacity of at least 1, a refill of at least 0, and a period of at least 1. `window <name> <limit> <span>` declares a sliding window, with a limit of at least 0 and a span of at least 1. Two policies may not share a name. `route <prefix> <policy>...` sends every key that starts with that prefix to those policies, in the order written; every policy must already be declared, and two routes may not share a prefix. `event <tick> <key>` is one arrival at that tick, and ticks never go backwards across the file. Once the first event appears no further `bucket`, `window` or `route` line may follow.

Each policy keeps one independent state per key. A key is limited by the route whose prefix it starts with and which is longest among those that match; a key no route matches is always allowed. When an event arrives, every policy on its route first advances to the event's tick, then every one of them is asked, and only when all of them allow it does each of them record it. A denied event changes no policy's stored allowance.

A token bucket holds `capacity` tokens and starts full when a key first reaches it. Advancing it to a tick adds `refill` tokens for every `per` ticks that passed since it last advanced for that key, without ever passing the capacity, and partial periods accumulate exactly: after `n` ticks the bucket holds `refill` times `n` divided by `per` more tokens than it did, and that fraction is never rounded away. It allows a request when it holds at least one whole token, and recording one spends exactly one.

A sliding window remembers the ticks of the requests it recorded for a key. Advancing it to a tick forgets every remembered tick at or before the tick minus the span, so the window covers the `span` ticks ending at the current one. It allows a request when fewer than `limit` ticks remain remembered, and recording one remembers this tick.

`replay` prints one line per event in log order: `<tick> <key> allow`, or `<tick> <key> deny <policy>` naming the first policy on the route, in the order the route wrote them, that refused. `summary` instead prints `<key> allowed=<a> denied=<d>` for every key that saw an event, in ascending key order, and then `total allowed=<a> denied=<d>`.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. `jobq` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/jobq.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the retry policy the simulator was built around, somewhere for a job that never succeeds to go, and a way to run one log under a policy that does not live in it. Everything `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is — the log grammar, the simulation, the `trace` and `summary` output, and every failure message and exit code — and the work spans the parser, the simulation, and the command.

`retry <max> <base>` joins the log's directives, parsed like `limit`: exactly two words after it, `<max>` a positive integer and `<base>` a non-negative one, at most one such line, and the same failures as the others, worded `expected retry <max> <base>`, `max must be a positive integer`, `base must be a non-negative integer` and `retry is declared twice`. The directive turns the policy on. With no `retry` line anywhere a job still gets one attempt and a failure is simply final, exactly as today.

Under a retry policy, an attempt that finishes `fail` goes back in the queue when its attempt number is below `<max>`, ready at the instant it failed plus `<base>` multiplied by two raised to the power of one less than that attempt number, so the first backoff is `<base>`, the second twice that, the third four times. A re-queued attempt competes for the worker like any other: it is taken when its ready time is the smallest, ties still break by submission order, and its start still waits out the rate limit. An attempt that finishes `fail` at attempt `<max>` is dead-lettered instead, at the instant it failed.

`dead` is a new mode. It prints one line per dead-lettered job in the order the jobs were written off, `<id> attempts=<n> at=<instant>`, and then a final line `total <k>` counting them. # jobq

A job-queue simulator with no dependencies. It reads a log from standard input and replays it on one worker against a clock that only moves when the simulation asks it to, so a run is the same on every machine and in every order.

## Layout

| File | What it owns |
| --- | --- |
| `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
| `src/parse.js` | the log grammar and the refusals it words, as `LogError` |
| `src/queue.js` | the simulation: what starts when, and what the rate limit holds back |
| `src/clock.js` | `createClock`, the monotonic clock the simulation advances by hand |

`test/jobq.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the policy files the examples name.

## The log

One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace. Every number is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign or a separator.

```
limit 2 10
job build 5 ok
job flaky 3 fail ok
submit 0 build
submit 0 flaky
```

`limit <starts> <window>` allows at most `<starts>` starts inside any window of `<window>` milliseconds, and may appear at most once. `job <id> <duration> <outcome>...` declares a job that occupies the worker for `<duration>` milliseconds and whose attempts turn out as the listed `ok` and `fail` words, the last of which repeats. An id is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. `submit <at> <id>` puts a declared job in the queue at that instant; a job may be submitted at most once.

## The simulation

The clock starts at 0 and one worker runs everything. Take the queued attempt with the smallest ready time, breaking ties by submission order, and advance the clock to that ready time. If a rate limit is in force and the last `<starts>` starts all fall inside the window ending now, advance the clock to the instant the oldest of them leaves it. The attempt starts at the clock's instant and finishes `<duration>` later, and the clock advances to that finish. A job of duration 0 finishes in the instant it starts. A failed attempt is simply over: nothing here retries it.

## Modes

- `trace` prints one line per attempt in the order the attempts started, `<start> <id> attempt=<n> <outcome> finish=<finish>`, and then a final `end <clock>` line.
- `summary` prints one line per submitted job in ascending id order, `<id> attempts=<n> <outcome of its last attempt>`, and then the same final `end <clock>` line.

A declared job nothing submits never runs and appears nowhere.

## Failures

Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure names its 1-based log line: `error: line 2: unknown directive cancel`. The messages are `expected limit <starts> <window>`, `expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...`, `expected submit <at> <id>`, `invalid job id <id>`, `invalid outcome <word>`, `<field> must be a non-negative integer` and `<field> must be a positive integer` naming `at`, `duration`, `starts` or `window`, `job <id> is declared twice`, `job <id> is submitted twice`, `limit is declared twice`, and `unknown directive <word>`. A `submit` line naming a job no `job` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown job <id>`. A malformed argument list is refused with the usage line.

## Known gaps

A failure is the end of a job: there is no retry, no backoff, and nowhere for a job that never succeeds to go. The rate limit and nothing else can be configured, it can only come from the log itself, and there is no way to run the same log under a different policy.

     1	/** The simulation: one worker and a rate limit on starts. */
     2	
     3	import { createClock } from './clock.js'
     4	
     5	/**
     6	 * Run every submission to a verdict.
     7	 * @param {Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>} jobs - the declared jobs.
     8	 * @param {{id: string, at: number}[]} submissions - the submissions, in input order.
     9	 * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}}} policy - the rate limit in force.
    10	 * @returns {{attempts: {start: number, id: string, attempt: number, outcome: string, finish: number}[], end: number}} the attempts in the order they started and the clock at the end.
    11	 */
    12	export function run(jobs, submissions, policy) {
    13	  const clock = createClock()
    14	  const queued = submissions.map((submission, order) => ({ ...submission, order, readyAt: submission.at, attempt: 0 }))
    15	  const attempts = []
    16	  const starts = []
    17	  while (queued.length > 0) {
    18	    let pick = 0
    19	    for (const [index, entry] of queued.entries()) {
    20	      const best = queued[pick]
    21	      if (entry.readyAt < best.readyAt || (entry.readyAt === best.readyAt && entry.order < best.order)) pick = index
    22	    }
    23	    const entry = queued.splice(pick, 1)[0]
    24	    clock.advanceTo(entry.readyAt)
    25	    if (policy.limit !== undefined && starts.length >= policy.limit.starts) {
    26	      const oldest = starts[starts.length - policy.limit.starts]
    27	      if (clock.now() - oldest < policy.limit.window) clock.advanceTo(oldest + policy.limit.window)
    28	    }
    29	    const job = jobs.get(entry.id)
    30	    const start = clock.now()
    31	    starts.push(start)
    32	    const attempt = entry.attempt + 1
    33	    const outcome = job.outcomes[Math.min(attempt, job.outcomes.length) - 1]
    34	    const finish = start + job.duration
    35	    clock.advanceTo(finish)
    36	    attempts.push({ start, id: entry.id, attempt, outcome, finish })
    37	  }
    38	  return { attempts, end: clock.now() }
    39	}

1: /** The log grammar: the directives, and the failures each one words. */
2: 
3: const ID = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: const DIGITS = /^[0-9]+$/
5: 
6: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line, or 0 when the failure names none. */
7: export class LogError extends Error {
8:   /**
9:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names no line.
10:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
11:    */
12:   constructor(line, message) {
13:     super(message)
14:     this.name = 'LogError'
15:     this.line = line
16:   }
17: }
18: 
19: /**
20:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
21:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
22:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
23:  */
24: export function splitLines(text) {
25:   const split = text.split('\n')
26:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
27:   return split
28: }
29: 
30: /** One field read as a non-negative integer, or the failure that names it. */
31: function count(line, field, word) {
32:   if (!DIGITS.test(word)) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a non-negative integer`)
33:   return Number(word)
34: }
35: 
36: /** One field read as a positive integer, or the failure that names it. */
37: function positive(line, field, word) {
38:   const value = count(line, field, word)
39:   if (value < 1) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a positive integer`)
40:   return value
41: }
42: 
43: /**
44:  * Parse the job log.
45:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
46:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}}} policy - the policy the log sets, edited in place.
47:  * @returns {{jobs: Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>, submissions: {id: string, at: number}[]}} the declared jobs and the submissions in input order.
48:  * @throws {LogError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
49:  */
50: export function parse(lines, policy) {
51:   const jobs = new Map()
52:   const submissions = []
53:   const submitted = new Map()
54:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
55:     const line = index + 1
56:     const text = raw.trim()
57:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
58:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
59:     if (words[0] === 'limit') {
60:       if (words.length !== 3) throw new LogError(line, 'expected limit <starts> <window>')
61:       if (policy.limit !== undefined) throw new LogError(line, 'limit is declared twice')
62:       policy.limit = { starts: positive(line, 'starts', words[1]), window: positive(line, 'window', words[2]) }
63:     } else if (words[0] === 'job') {
64:       if (words.length < 4) throw new LogError(line, 'expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...')
65:       const id = words[1]
66:       if (!ID.test(id)) throw new LogError(line, `invalid job id ${id}`)
67:       if (jobs.has(id)) throw new LogError(line, `job ${id} is declared twice`)
68:       const duration = count(line, 'duration', words[2])
69:       for (const outcome of words.slice(3)) {
70:         if (outcome !== 'ok' && outcome !== 'fail') throw new LogError(line, `invalid outcome ${outcome}`)
71:       }
72:       jobs.set(id, { id, duration, outcomes: words.slice(3) })
73:     } else if (words[0] === 'submit') {
74:       if (words.length !== 3) throw new LogError(line, 'expected submit <at> <id>')
75:       const at = count(line, 'at', words[1])
76:       const id = words[2]
77:       if (!ID.test(id)) throw new LogError(line, `invalid job id ${id}`)
78:       if (submitted.has(id)) throw new LogError(line, `job ${id} is submitted twice`)
79:       submitted.set(id, line)
80:       submissions.push({ id, at })
81:     } else {
82:       throw new LogError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
83:     }
84:   }
85:   for (const { id } of submissions) {
86:     if (!jobs.has(id)) throw new LogError(0, `unknown job ${id}`)
87:   }
88:   return { jobs, submissions }
89: }

1: /** The simulation: one worker and a rate limit on starts. */
2: 
3: import { createClock } from './clock.js'
4: 
5: /**
6:  * Run every submission to a verdict.
7:  * @param {Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>} jobs - the declared jobs.
8:  * @param {{id: string, at: number}[]} submissions - the submissions, in input order.
9:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}}} policy - the rate limit in force.
10:  * @returns {{attempts: {start: number, id: string, attempt: number, outcome: string, finish: number}[], end: number}} the attempts in the order they started and the clock at the end.
11:  */
12: export function run(jobs, submissions, policy) {
13:   const clock = createClock()
14:   const queued = submissions.map((submission, order) => ({ ...submission, order, readyAt: submission.at, attempt: 0 }))
15:   const attempts = []
16:   const starts = []
17:   while (queued.length > 0) {
18:     let pick = 0
19:     for (const [index, entry] of queued.entries()) {
20:       const best = queued[pick]
21:       if (entry.readyAt < best.readyAt || (entry.readyAt === best.readyAt && entry.order < best.order)) pick = index
22:     }
23:     const entry = queued.splice(pick, 1)[0]
24:     clock.advanceTo(entry.readyAt)
25:     if (policy.limit !== undefined && starts.length >= policy.limit.starts) {
26:       const oldest = starts[starts.length - policy.limit.starts]
27:       if (clock.now() - oldest < policy.limit.window) clock.advanceTo(oldest + policy.limit.window)
28:     }
29:     const job = jobs.get(entry.id)
30:     const start = clock.now()
31:     starts.push(start)
32:     const attempt = entry.attempt + 1
33:     const outcome = job.outcomes[Math.min(attempt, job.outcomes.length) - 1]
34:     const finish = start + job.duration
35:     clock.advanceTo(finish)
36:     attempts.push({ start, id: entry.id, attempt, outcome, finish })
37:   }
38:   return { attempts, end: clock.now() }
39: }

`retry <max> <base>` joins the log's directives, parsed like `limit`: exactly two words after it, `<max>` a positive integer and `<base>` a non-negative one, at most one such line, and the same failures as the others, worded `expected retry <max> <base>`, `max must be a positive integer`, `base must be a non-negative integer` and `retry is declared twice`. The directive turns the policy on. With no `retry` line anywhere a job still gets one attempt and a failure is simply final, exactly as today.

Under a retry policy, an attempt that finishes `fail` goes back in the queue when its attempt number is below `<max>`, ready at the instant it failed plus `<base>` multiplied by two raised to the power of one less than that attempt number, so the first backoff is `<base>`, the second twice that, the third four times. A re-queued attempt competes for the worker like any other: it is taken when its ready time is the smallest, ties still break by submission order, and its start still waits out the rate limit. An attempt that finishes `fail` at attempt `<max>` is dead-lettered instead, at the instant it failed.

`dead` is a new mode. It prints one line per dead-lettered job in the order the jobs were written off, `<id> attempts=<n> at=<instant>`, and then a final line `total <k>` counting them. In `summary`, a dead-lettered job reads `dead` in place of its last attempt's outcome; every other job reads that outcome as before.

Every mode takes an optional second argument naming a policy file, so the usage line becomes `error: usage: cli.js trace|summary|dead [<policy>]`. A policy file holds `limit` and `retry` lines and nothing else, read under the log's own grammar, with a line trimmed and an empty one or one starting with `#` ignored. It is read before the log, so its failures come first, and a directive it sets is already in force when the log is parsed: a log that sets the same directive fails at the log's own line with `limit is declared twice` or `retry is declared twice`. A policy file's own failures are worded `error: <policy>: line N: ` followed by the message the same directive would give in the log, with `unknown directive <word>` for anything that is not `limit` or `retry`, and N counting the policy file's own lines from 1. A policy file that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read policy <path>`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.
